# Fugaro CLI reference

Every command and flag `fugaro` ships, generated from the command tree
(`internal/cli.NewRootCmd`) by `go run ./ee/clidoc`. Cobra's own `help`
and `completion` commands, the root's `-v, --verbose` and `--version`

hides are not listed: they are internal, and a hidden command is not user
documentation.

## `fugaro ab`

Report model A/B results: pairs, wins, cost and the recommendation per group

Report model A/B results from the runs the launcher sampled.

A sampled task launches a champion (the run the developer sees) and a
challenger (the same task, at the same commit, on another coder model, run as a
shadow that pushes nothing and opens nothing). Both records carry the pair, and
this command scores the pairs from those records and from what the repository's
judge runs wrote under their own prefixes: no model call is made here, and the
same records and verdicts always give the same table. A pair at Critical counts
only once a judge has decided it (D561), and every other mode shows the judge's
verdict beside the hard signals it is ranked on.

Rows are one per rigor mode x tier x model pair. A pair the arms do not make --
a different start commit, mode, tier or recipe, or an arm that never started --
is in no figure at all. WINS and LOSSES are the challenger's; a TIE decided
nothing and no figure is drawn from one. HALTS is each arm's halt count: a halt
is already a loss, and the count says how often a limit rather than the work
decided a pair. COST is the median pair cost ratio, the challenger's model
dollars over the champion's. JUDGE FAMILY is the family of the model that judged
the group's pairs -- a Claude ID is anthropic, a provider model's family is its
ID's vendor prefix -- and SAME FAMILY says one of them is an arm's own, which
blindness does not remove (D553). UNJUDGED counts the pairs no judge has decided
and TRUNCATED those whose patch was cut short and can never be judged.

ADVICE is D565's rule at the mode's exchange rate: the challenger is recommended
when it is clearly better (the lower bound of its win share above a half) and its
median cost ratio is within the mode's rate, or when it is not worse (the upper
bound of its loss share below 0.6) and cheaper; otherwise the champion stays. A
row with fewer than 20 decisive pairs says no conclusion rather than
approximating one. Nothing here changes a default: this is a report, not a
switch.

No person, repository or task text reaches the output: a row is a mode, a tier and
two coder models, with the family of the model that judged them.

--since is how far back the read goes (default 30d: a day count, a Go duration,
or 0 for no bound). --json prints {project, source, since, until, rows[{mode,
tier, champion, challenger, pairs, wins, losses, ties, champion_halts,
challenger_halts, champion_follow_ups, judge_families, judge_same_family,
unjudged, truncated, recommendation{decision, rule, decisive, p, win_share_lo,
win_share_hi, median_cost_ratio, exchange_rate}}], warnings};
median_cost_ratio is null when no pair of the group carried both arms' costs,
and judge_families is empty when no judge has decided a pair of the group.

Usage: `fugaro ab`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for ab |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | only this repository (owner/name) |
| `--since` | string | `30d` | no | how far back to read: Nd, a Go duration, or 0 for no bound |

## `fugaro accounts add`

Declare a named Claude account and the repositories its token may be used by

Declare a named Claude OAuth account in this project, and converge the
installation on it.

It writes claude_accounts.<name>.allow_data_to — the repositories the account's
token may be used by, and the field every other rule is built on — and adds the
name to one profile's claude_accounts, so the profile's jobs may serve it.

--repos defaults to this checkout's origin repository. A profile that lists
accounts must write its own allow_repos, and every account it lists must cover
every repository on it: an account that covers less is refused before the file
is touched, naming the repositories it is missing, because widening the account
silently is what that rule exists to prevent.

--type declares the name as a typed credential as well, in this prefix's
credentials block: the entry that lets a pool list the name as a member
(fugaro accounts pool add). claude-oauth is the type this command's token step
serves. vertex is built in and is never defined, and the two types the spec
lists as future work are refused in words that say so. A type whose key no
command stores yet is refused too: the entry would name a credential no run
could authenticate with. Without the flag nothing but claude_accounts and the
profile is written, which is what this command has always done.

Then it converges, in one command and behind the one sentence it prints: the
token is stored project-wide as a new version of the account's own secret, the
account's broken mark is cleared, and the publisher, the job set and this
checkout's repository root are converged — the same stages fugaro update runs,
invoked here rather than forked. It ends on the line that says what is left,
which is a fugaro run and never an update.

--claude runs Anthropic's own claude setup-token on your own terminal first,
so the login is the one you would have run yourself: it gets your stdin, stdout
and stderr, and fugaro reads none of what it prints. The token is then read at
the hidden prompt below, exactly as it is without the flag — that prompt is the
only source of the value, so a login you cancelled or that failed costs one
paste rather than the command. A login that failed stores nothing and still
leaves you the prompt.

Run it at your own terminal. This file decides where a credential may be sent
and this command then stores the token itself, so in a project whose marks say
it is managed the token is written for YOU and nobody else: before the token
prompt it prints the repositories the token may be used by and says that a job
on those repositories can read it. Nothing is asked — the terminal is what makes
a run yours, and --yes does not stand in for one — so a pipe and a run with no
terminal are refused before a byte is written.

A coding agent's session may still declare a bounded account: the repositories
it names are the only ones the token may be used by, and none of them is beyond
this checkout. The token is not written for it, because a secret is the one
step no plan admits.

Usage: `fugaro accounts add NAME`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--ask` | bool | `false` | no | in a project whose marks say it is managed, ask the confirmation this declaration would otherwise get instead of writing on the gate's verdict: a managed project asks nothing by default, and this is the flag that puts the question back. Refused where nobody can answer it (a coding agent's session, a pipe); a no-op with a sentence in a project that is not managed; refused beside --yes |
| `--claude` | bool | `false` | no | run Anthropic's own claude setup-token login on this terminal first, then paste the token at the hidden prompt |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for add |
| `--profile` | string | "" | no | the profile whose claude_accounts gains the name (default: the only profile, when there is exactly one) |
| `--repos` | string | "" | no | the repositories the token may be used by, as owner/name,owner/name (default: this checkout's origin) |
| `--type` | string | "" | no | declare the name as a typed credential too, so a craft or a pool may spend it: claude-oauth, the one type this command's token step serves (without it, the name is declared in claude_accounts alone, as it always was) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the run without a prompt: it answers the converge's own questions and never makes a run the owner at their own terminal on a managed project |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro accounts allow`

Add repositories to a named Claude account's allow-list (claude_accounts.NAME.allow_data_to)

Add each REPO to claude_accounts.NAME.allow_data_to, the list of
repositories the account's token may be used by, and nothing else.

A NAME the config does not declare yet is declared here with the repositories
this run names: allow is the first form of the pair, so an account whose
token may be spent from one repository needs no second command. A NAME it does
declare keeps the repositories its list already holds — the edit appends the
ones named, so a run that repeats an entry writes nothing.

The list is the per-repository decision the published policy's accounts block
is derived from: a profile serves the account to its jobs, and this list is
what bounds the token of each of them. Adding a repository is therefore a
widening of where the token may be spent, and it is read back by the owner's
own publish rather than by this command — nothing here reaches the cloud.

The repositories are written as owner/name, the shape the loader holds this
list to. A repository the file already names is left where it is, and the
sentence above the diff prints the list the file ends up with, not the one the
command line named.

This is a local file edit. It ends on one line: next: fugaro update — the
published policy's accounts block is derived from this list, so the change
reaches the project's runs in that run and not before it.

Usage: `fugaro accounts allow NAME REPO...`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for allow |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the change without a prompt |

## `fugaro accounts clear`

Clear one account's broken or exhausted credential mark, after replacing its token

Clear one Claude account's credential mark, so the cascade may route work to it
again. This is an operator's command: it writes the project's own database,
acting as you (ADC), and it is the only thing that ends a broken mark.

Only the two states an operator's action is what ends may be cleared:

  broken     the service saw a 401 (D139) and nothing clears it on its own.
             Replace the token first, then clear the mark here.
  exhausted  the account reported a usage limit and holds until its reset time.

A backed-off mark is refused: a probe is what clears it (C1.12), and clearing it
by hand would route real work to a credential that has not answered since it was
held. A state this Fugaro does not know is refused too, because clearing it
could take off a hold a newer release placed.

The write is one node — creds/marks/NAME, in this installation's own database —
and it is conditional on the value read (PutIfMatch), so a mark the service
changed at the same moment is not lost: the write re-reads the mark and clears
it only while its state is still the one this run announced, so a 401 the
service recorded while you were reading is left for its own decision rather
than taken off with the hold you asked for.

NAME is "default" (the repository's own unnamed claude-oauth-token secret), a
claude_accounts name of the selected project config, or an account the database
already carries a mark for — a mark is the account existing, and a name with
none of the three is refused rather than written, so a typo cannot leave a mark
node for a credential that does not exist. (A mark whose name this checkout's
claude_accounts does not list is the ordinary case for a project several
checkouts share: claude_accounts is per-checkout and never published, while the
marks are the project's own. fugaro doctor names such marks, so its fix has
to work here.) Nothing reads or prints a token value, a secret ID or a prefix
of one: names and states only.

This command is run by a person in the sense that it acts as you, with your own
credentials, on your own installation's database — but it is not one of the
commands that refuse a coding agent's session. It records no owner decision and
approves nothing: it takes off a hold the service placed, on a credential you
have already replaced the token for, and the service marks it broken again if
the token is still refused. fugaro budget set and fugaro budget kill — the
same kind of write to the same database, with the same credentials — refuse no
agent either, and fugaro allow-delete and fugaro managed flag, which do, are
commands whose own output is an approval of a later cloud change.

Usage: `fugaro accounts clear NAME`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for clear |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | skip the typed confirmation (read what it does first) |

## `fugaro accounts deny`

Remove repositories from a named Claude account's allow-list

Remove each REPO from claude_accounts.NAME.allow_data_to, so the
account's token may no longer be used by it.

A repository the list does not name is not an error and not a write: the
command says there is no change, because the state it was asked for is the
state the file is in.

An account a profile lists must cover every repository that profile admits —
the profile's repositories are the intersection of the two lists — so a
removal that would leave the profile admitting a repository the account no
longer covers is refused, naming the repository and the profile, with nothing
written. The remedy is to narrow the profile's own allow_repos, or to leave
the entry where it is.

This is a local file edit. It ends on one line: next: fugaro update — the
published policy's accounts block is derived from this list, so the change
reaches the project's runs in that run and not before it.

## `fugaro accounts ls`

List the named Claude accounts (claude_accounts in the local config) a repository may use with fugaro run --token

List the names fugaro run --token NAME (and a repository's own agent.oauth_token)
accept for a repository: "default" (the repository's own unnamed
claude-oauth-token secret, always allowed) first, then every claude_accounts
name in the local config whose allow_data_to lists the repository, sorted
(config.AllowedClaudeAccounts, the one place that decides the question).

The names are a local, read-only lookup, offline whenever a project config is
already selected on this machine: it reads the local config file the CLI would
otherwise select for a cloud command, and never calls Secret Manager, never
reads or prints a token value, only names.

The state column is not local. When the selected project has a Firebase budget
backend (budget.rtdb_url, which fugaro update --firebase-project <gcp-project-id> writes), each account's
credential state is read from that database as you, with your Application
Default Credentials — the creds/marks subtree the credentials service writes,
which an admin's rules grant the read of — and printed beside the name as
available, exhausted until T, backed off or broken. A project with no backend,
and a machine where no project config could be selected, answer with the names
alone and a note saying why: the command never turns "could not read" into
"every account is available".

That read is bounded: five seconds for the whole of it (the token source, the
project check and the marks), one attempt per call, and no retry. A database
that is unreachable rather than refusing — a laptop offline, a firewall that
drops — therefore costs this command seconds, not the per-call timeout twice,
and the names are printed with a note saying the states could not be read.

--json's "complete" is false when no project config could be selected for a
reason other than an explicit --config/--project/$FUGARO_CONFIG/$FUGARO_PROJECT
(several project configs with nothing to pick one, for example): "accounts"
is then "default" alone, which may be short the repository's real
claude_accounts, not a true answer that none are configured; "note" says why.

Usage: `fugaro accounts ls`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |

| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |

## `fugaro accounts pool add`

Declare a pool with these members, in this order

Declare pools.<NAME> in this project: the credentials it walks, in the order it
walks them.

The members are credential names the same config defines (fugaro accounts ls
names the accounts; the Claude OAuth ones a credential entry each), and they are
written in the order given — failover tries them in that order and round-robin
starts from the first. A credential the config does not define, a repeated
member, a name this command may not use and a strategy that is not failover or
round-robin are all refused before the file is touched.

--strategy failover (the default) or round-robin. A pool that already exists
keeps the strategy it has when the flag is left out, and this command replaces
its members with the list on the command line: it is the whole list every time,
so a member you leave out is dropped.

Run it at your own terminal: a pool decides where a project's calls may be
spent and whose key they may carry, so a coding agent's session is refused,
--yes included.

Usage: `fugaro accounts pool add NAME MEMBER...`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for add |
| `--strategy` | string | "" | no | how the pool walks its members: failover (the default: try them in order) or round-robin (share the load). Left out, a pool that exists keeps the strategy it has |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the write without a prompt |

## `fugaro accounts pool ls`

List the named pools and the members each one walks

List the pools the installation's own config defines (pools, docs/model-crafts/spec.md §2): each pool's
strategy, its members in the order it walks them, and which half of a run
serves them.

An OpenRouter or Vertex member is served by a run's own gateway; a Claude OAuth
or Anthropic-key member by the credentials service, which selects by tier
(OAuth before key: D154). A pool whose members need both is one that can only
fail over where the credential is chosen again, at a stage boundary.

The read is offline: it reads the selected project's config file and reaches no
bucket, no database and no host.

## `fugaro accounts pool rm`

## `fugaro accounts rm`

Remove a named Claude account, its secret and the job that served it

Remove a named Claude OAuth account from this project and converge the
installation on its absence.

The account is removed in the order that cannot strand a running job. While a
profile still lists it, the command refuses — naming each profile — because a
profile's claude_accounts is a job this installation has deployed, and removing
the account under a live job leaves a job the policy cannot describe:
fugaro accounts rm NAME --profile PROFILE takes the name out of that profile's
list alone, and this command removes the declaration, the secret and the job
once no profile lists it.

If a repository's committed fugaro.yaml still names the account in
agent.oauth_token, the command warns instead, naming the repository and the run
that stops at launch: that file belongs to the repository and not to this
installation, so your own edit is not blocked by one this command cannot write.

Removing the declaration also deletes the secret claude-oauth-token-<name>
through Secret Manager's own delete. That delete cannot be undone — Secret
Manager keeps no grace period for a secret — and the copy of the credential
left behind is the token at the provider. The secret's ID is named in the
sentence this run prints before it goes, and the command says plainly that deleting the
secret does not revoke the token at the provider: it stays valid until it
expires or you revoke it in Anthropic's own console, which no command here
reaches.

Then it converges, in the same command and after that one sentence: the
policy node the account was published in, the job set and this checkout's
repository root, through the stages fugaro update runs.

If the delete fails after the config was written, the config is put back the
way it was and the command stops: an account whose declaration is gone while
its secret is still there is the one state this command may not leave behind.

Run it at your own terminal: this command deletes a credential, so a coding
agent's session is refused, --yes included — a managed project's gate refuses
the removal too, because the refs and the checkouts record its referrer check
reads are documents the session writes, so no read here answers for what origin
carries.

Usage: `fugaro accounts rm NAME`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for rm |
| `--profile` | string | "" | no | the profile whose claude_accounts loses the name (a profile that lists accounts is taken out of it one at a time) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the removal without a prompt |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro allow-delete`

Record the objects a run may delete or replace, by address (the project's owner)

Record which Terraform addresses the project's owner approves for deletion or
replacement, and which object at each address is approved, in a managed
project's fugaro/allow-delete.json at the root of the runs bucket. An approval
lives in that object and nowhere else: this command is Fugaro's only writer of
it, with the operator's own credentials.

An argument is an address and the identity of the object approved there,
written as ADDRESS=IDENTITY: the Terraform address a plan reports, as in
google_cloud_run_v2_job.web or module.web.google_storage_bucket.data,
followed by the identity a refused managed apply printed for the object that
address removes, as in

  fugaro allow-delete 'module.web.google_storage_bucket.data=type=google_storage_bucket project=proj-1234 name=data id=data-bucket instance=2026-01-02T03:04:05.678Z'

An approval is of one object and not of the address: the same address carrying
another object later — another name, a renamed or replaced resource, one moved
in from elsewhere — is not approved by it, so an entry an earlier apply already
used admits nothing more. The identity is compared character for character with
the one the plan's before view shows, so copy it from the refusal rather than
retyping it. A refusal prints it inside a sentence of its own, so copy the
identity up to and not including the ')' that closes that sentence's
parenthetical — pasting that bracket as well is forgiven, once, since the
sentence put it there; one matched pair of double quotes is stripped the same
way, because a shell or a message may have added them (a quote at one end only
is a character of the identity, and is kept). What is not forgiven is any other
parenthesis: an identity holds none — a value's '(' and ')' are escaped with
everything else this program's printers would touch — so an argument that still
holds one is refused rather than recorded as an entry that would match no
removal. The two ends agree byte for byte because the identity is written in an
escaped form — a space in a value as \x20, a backslash as \\, a parenthesis as
\x28 and \x29, any other byte with no printable form as \xHH, and every byte a
shell reads in a way of its own — a separator, a pipe, a redirection, a
substitution, a quote, a glob, an expansion — as \xHH as well, so that what a
refusal prints holds no byte that can begin, end or continue a command, and is
exactly what a plan shows. Two bytes a shell rewrites are in it all the same,
because the form needs them: the single space between two parts, and the
backslash that introduces an escape. A paste that does not keep those two whole
arrives here as several arguments and is refused rather than recorded — nothing
is written, and no entry is made that would match no removal — but the identity
has to reach this command as one argument, byte for byte as the plan shows it,
for the loop to close. An identity longer than 8192
characters is refused here and by the plan: no refusal prints one, and the plan
refuses the removal rather than matching a printed part of it, so recording it
would be an approval that deletes nothing.

What the identity tells apart, and what it does not, said here rather than left
to be discovered. For the seven managed types whose state carries a value the
provider mints once per instance — a bucket's time_created, a secret's or an
artifact repository's create_time, a Cloud Run job's or an API key's uid, a
service account's unique_id, a bucket object's generation — the identity
carries that value, so an object of one of those types deleted and then created
again under the same name at the same address carries a DIFFERENT identity and
this entry no longer approves its removal. It does not for the seven types that
have no such value: a Cloud Scheduler job, a project service, and the five
*_iam_member types, whose whole state is the grant they carry. For those the
identity is the named object, and a re-creation under the same name at the same
address is approved by the entry that named it. The provider's own id is not
one of the instance values: for every managed type it is derived from the
configured name (an API key's id is projects/P/locations/global/keys/NAME).
If the difference matters for a resource of the second kind, review the list
rather than rely on the entry having been used up.

Nothing else is recorded — no note and no reason: the object's own version
history is the record of who approved what and when, and the identity is what
the approved delete is identified by.

Run it in your own terminal, as an operator, with your own credentials. Pass
the entries to approve, and they replace the list: an invocation that leaves an
entry out removes that approval, so the command names the entries it would drop
and asks for the project's name before writing such a list. With no arguments
the command prints the list — each entry in the same ADDRESS=IDENTITY form —
and writes nothing; it never empties the list, because an empty list is what an
absent one already means. A printed line is one you can paste back as far as its
IDENTITY half goes: the command that recorded the entry escaped it, so the
printers leave it alone and a line inside the listing's own bound carries it
back byte for byte. The address half is the plan's own — not escaped here and
not bounded here — so an address holding a tab, a run of spaces or a byte
outside printable ASCII is printed as the printers rewrite it: that line is not
the entry, and pasting it back records an entry about an address no plan has,
which the plan refuses rather than deleting anything. A line longer than twice
the identity's own bound is printed through the bounded sanitiser instead, cut
and marked as cut: what you read there is visibly a text and not an entry. The
entry itself is unchanged in the object either way.

What the object is for: a run's own credentials cannot write it, and the
deployer account a managed apply impersonates will not be able to (D75, Task
1.5), so a managed apply can take its allow-list from the owner's object
instead of from the command line of whatever session is applying: fugaro
managed apply reads this object and takes no address flag of its own, so the
session that applies cannot widen the list. (the converge still honours its own
--allow-delete on its own command line, where the addresses go to tf.Guard
directly.) What this does not do: a coding agent's session holds the
operator's credentials, so it can write this object directly (gcloud storage
cp) or unset its agent marker and run this command itself. The refusal below is a speed bump against
an agent that uses the program, not a boundary against one that goes around it
(SECURITY.md records the wider Owner/Editor bypass).

On a project that is not managed, this writes an object nothing reads: the
check below is that the bucket is the project's own runs bucket, which every
installation has, not that the project is Fugaro-managed.

The list is read fail-closed: an absent object, an empty one, one naming
another project, one written by an older Fugaro (its addresses carry no
identities, so nothing in it says which object was approved), one whose
identities are an earlier build's (an entry that names the object without the
per-instance value its type has matches no removal the gate identifies, so it
approves nothing — re-approve it from a current refusal), one whose fields
are not exactly the ones this command writes, or one this package cannot read
is no entries — and no entries refuses every delete and replacement rather
than permitting them. The write is fail-closed too: if the current list cannot
be read, nothing is written, and the write is conditioned on the object being
unchanged since that read, so a concurrent write is never silently overwritten
(run the command again).

Usage: `fugaro allow-delete [ADDRESS=IDENTITY...]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for allow-delete |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro artifacts`

List and download what an artifact run delivered

Read and fetch the files a `mode: artifact` run put in the runs bucket.

Both subcommands read the run's result.json, never a bucket listing: ls prints
the record's own table, and get is the object — so an artifact the record names
and the bucket no longer holds (they expire with the run, runs_days) is a
recorded row that ls shows and a `get` that says exactly that.

The record was written by an untrusted, model-driven run, so get treats every
name in it as hostile: it downloads into a fresh directory it creates
(./<run>-artifacts/, with --out naming that directory's parent), refuses a name
that is absolute, walks out of that directory or begins with a dot, refuses to
overwrite an existing file without --force, and verifies the recorded size and
sha256 as the bytes arrive, leaving nothing behind when they do not match.
What it writes is never opened, executed or unpacked.

Usage: `fugaro artifacts`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for artifacts |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro artifacts get` -- Download a run's artifacts, verifying them against its record
- `fugaro artifacts ls` -- List what a run's record says it delivered

## `fugaro artifacts get`

Download a run's artifacts, verifying them against its record

Download one artifact NAME, or every artifact the record lists when NAME is
omitted, verifying each one's size and sha256 against the run's result.json as
the bytes arrive. RUN is a run ID, <repo-slug>/<run-id>, or the last four or
more characters of a run ID. A mismatch is an error naming both hashes, and
nothing is written — not even the file the download streamed into.

The destination is a fresh directory this command creates,
./<run-id>-artifacts/ unless --out names another parent for it. A name in the
record that is absolute, walks out of that directory, begins with a dot or
holds a control character is refused — a refusal, never a flattened name.
An existing file needs --force to be replaced.

Nothing downloaded is ever opened, executed or unpacked: the recorded content
type, the size and the sha256 are printed, and that is all. The sha256 proves
the bytes are the bytes the run uploaded; it is not tamper evidence.

Usage: `fugaro artifacts get RUN [NAME]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--force` | bool | `false` | no | replace a file that is already at a destination path |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for get |
| `--out` | string | "" | no | the directory to create the run's artifact directory in (default: the working directory) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | the repository RUN belongs to (owner/name, or a path inside its checkout; needed only for a bare run ID) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro artifacts ls`

List what a run's record says it delivered

List the artifacts RUN (a run ID, <repo-slug>/<run-id>, or the last four or
more characters of a run ID) recorded in its result.json: name, recorded
size, short sha256, recorded content type and the probe's verdict. The
record is shown as it is — a name `get` cannot retrieve is listed with the
reason, never filtered out, and a missing object is not ls's to hide: ls is
the record, get is the object.

--json prints the record's artifact list verbatim.

List the compute backends an installation can run its jobs on

## `fugaro backends ls`

List the compute backends this fugaro knows and which one the project uses

List the compute backends a project config's backend: key may name, and
which one the selected project uses:

  cloud-run    Cloud Run jobs (the default, and the one every installation
               runs on today)
  cloud-batch  Cloud Batch jobs, one VM per run (the VM backend)

A config that names no backend runs on cloud-run. A config that names
cloud-batch is ACCEPTED: fugaro doctor reports the Batch checks for an
installation that selects it -- the Compute and Batch APIs, the preloaded boot
image and the socket gid it records beside it, the network and subnetwork a
run's VMs are placed in, the log isolation, the run accounts and their grants,
the price table and the reaper -- and FAILS until every one of them passes.
What doctor does is report: fugaro run reads none of those checks, so it does
not hold a launch back, and an installation that selects the name before it is
provisioned runs anyway (its output stays in _Default and its VMs are left to
the job's own duration). Run fugaro doctor first, rather than reading a green
one as a fence around the launcher.

This is a local, read-only lookup: it reads the project config and the backend
names internal/backend defines, and it calls no cloud API. With --json it
prints one object instead of two lines, carrying the list, the selected project
and the name its config selects.

Usage: `fugaro backends ls`

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for ls |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |

## `fugaro backlog`

File a backlog item, read the backlog, regenerate its index

Read the backlog in docs/backlog/, file an item into it, and regenerate
its index.

The backlog is one Markdown file per item, named `<id>-<slug>.md`, beside
the generated index README.md and the hand-written format FORMAT.md. The
naming rule is what lets two pull requests file an item at once: they write
two differently named files, and the merge is a union of disjoint files
rather than a conflict (D26). `add` writes one item under that rule and
refuses the one the folder already holds — the same title filed twice on
the same day. The index is derived state — regenerated,
never merged by hand — so two branches that regenerated it at once are
reconciled by re-running `fugaro backlog index`, and never by merging the
file (D28). `add` regenerates it in the same commit that files the item;
`index` regenerates it alone; `list` writes nothing and prints what the
index would say.

Nothing here reaches a network, a credential or an installation: the items
and the index are files in this checkout.

Usage: `fugaro backlog`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for backlog |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro backlog add` -- File an item in docs/backlog/ and regenerate the index
- `fugaro backlog index` -- Regenerate docs/backlog/README.md from the item files beside it
- `fugaro backlog list` -- Print the backlog's items as the index lists them

## `fugaro backlog add`

File an item in docs/backlog/ and regenerate the index

File an item, and regenerate the index beside it.

The item takes the next id for the day it is filed (D26) and is written
as `<id>-<slug>.md`, with the eight front-matter fields the format
requires (D27). The index is regenerated in the same command, so the
commit that files an item is the commit that regenerates the index.

--title and --why are required, and so is --filed-by: an item is not a
title with no text, and who filed it is one of the eight fields. An item
is committed, so a --filed-by with an @ in it records `unknown`. --what
defaults to the title, and --done and --link are written when given.

An item filed by hand records `mode: none` — no run chose a mode for it.
--mode names the mode a run resolved when the item is about one, and
--filed-in says where it came from: `hand`, `run:<run id>` or
`pr:<number>`.

Usage: `fugaro backlog add`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--area` | string | `repo` | no | the area the item is about: an area name, project or repo |
| `--date` | string | "" | no | the day it is filed, as YYYY-MM-DD; today when empty |
| `--dir` | string | `docs/backlog` | no | the folder the item files live in |
| `--done` | string | "" | no | what done looks like |
| `--filed-by` | string | "" | no | who filed it: the run's launcher, or your login (required) |
| `--filed-in` | string | `hand` | no | where it came from: hand, run:<run id> or pr:<number> |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for add |
| `--link` | stringArray | `[]` | no | a link for the item's Links section (repeatable) |
| `--mode` | string | `none` | no | the mode a run resolved; none for an item filed by hand |
| `--title` | string | "" | no | the item's title, one line (required) |
| `--what` | string | "" | no | what was left open; the title when empty |
| `--why` | string | "" | no | why it is left open (required) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro backlog index`

Regenerate docs/backlog/README.md from the item files beside it

Regenerate the backlog's index from the item files.

The index lists one row per item — the id linked to its file, the title,
the mode, the area, the status, who filed it and the date — sorted by id,
with the closed and dropped rows grouped under the open ones, under a
count line (D28). It is written to <dir>/README.md, and it is the only
file this command touches.

The document is a pure function of the item files: every date in it comes
from the item that carries it and no clock is read, so regenerating an
unchanged folder rewrites the same bytes and a regeneration in review
diffs only where an item changed (D27). A pull request that adds an item
runs this in the same commit, and a test in internal/cli fails on an index
that is not current — which is why the file is never merged by hand.

Usage: `fugaro backlog index`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--dir` | string | `docs/backlog` | no | the folder the item files live in |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for index |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro backlog list`

Print the backlog's items as the index lists them

Print the backlog's items.

The output is the index itself, rendered from the item files rather than
read back from README.md: a stale index on disk cannot change what this
prints, and a reader who sees a difference between the two has found the
file that needs `fugaro backlog index`.

--json prints one document instead: {dir, items[{id, title, mode, area,
status, filed_by, filed_in, date, path}], open, closed, dropped}, indented.
The rows are the index's own rows in the index's own order, and the three
counts are the count line's own figures, so a screen shows what the
Markdown says rather than a second reading of the folder.

Nothing is written, and nothing is reached over the network: a folder that
does not exist is an error rather than an empty backlog.

Usage: `fugaro backlog list`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--dir` | string | `docs/backlog` | no | the folder the item files live in |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for list |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro budget`

Show and change the project's model-spend caps and kill switches

Look at and change the project's budget: the caps, today's counters, the kill
switches and the runs in flight, kept in the project's Firebase Realtime
Database (design §8). show needs the Viewer role on the Firebase project;
set, kill and resume need the budget-admin role (the project's owners and
editors, and terraform.budget_admins). preview needs the Viewer role too,
and reads the project's recipes from the runs bucket as recipes ls does,
which a plain project Viewer cannot (see docs/gcp-setup.md).

Usage: `fugaro budget`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for budget |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro budget kill` -- Halt every run of the project, of one repository or of one workspace (budget admins)
- `fugaro budget preview` -- Estimate a batch's worst-case model spend against today's caps
- `fugaro budget prices` -- Show the effective model price table, offline
- `fugaro budget resume` -- Clear a kill switch (budget admins)
- `fugaro budget set` -- Set a cap, the lease limit or the mode (budget admins)
- `fugaro budget show` -- Show caps, today's counters, kill switches, headroom and the runs in flight

## `fugaro budget kill`

Halt every run of the project, of one repository or of one workspace (budget admins)

Set the project's kill switch (--all), one repository's (--repo [owner/name]) or
one workspace's (--workspace <name>), recording who, when and why. --repo with
no value means the repository this checkout belongs to, as it does for set. show
takes owner/name (its empty --repo means no repository filter, not a checkout),
and preview already means this checkout's repository without the flag.
Runs in flight halt within seconds (a run in its last stage finishes pushing
its work first) and new runs refuse. Nothing is asked for it: halting runs
spends nothing, and only a resume is a raise. --workspace sets the stop flag
of the workspace's own service, in the workspace's own database, so every
member's runs that reach it with its shared credentials halt, and nothing of
a member's own — its credentials, its caps, its sign-in, its runs that never
reach the workspace — is touched.

Usage: `fugaro budget kill (--all | --repo [owner/name] | --workspace <name>) [--reason TEXT]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--all` | bool | `false` | no | the whole project |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for kill |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--reason` | string | "" | no | why (recorded, shown by budget show and watch) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | one repository, given as owner/name or a path inside its checkout (no value: this checkout's origin) |
| `--workspace` | string | "" | no | one workspace, named as its own project is; its own service's stop flag, in the workspace's own database, so the project it names has to declare one (workspace_members) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | accepted and ignored: this command asks nothing |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro budget preview`

Estimate a batch's worst-case model spend against today's caps

Estimate what N runs of a recipe may cost at most, and how that compares
with today's remaining daily caps. It is a ceiling, not a forecast: a run
is bounded by the smaller of budget.per_run_usd and the recipe's most
stages times the repository's agent.max_budget_usd.

--mode asks for a rigor mode for the figures, as fugaro run --mode asks
for one for a run, and takes the same vocabulary. It may raise the mode
the repository resolves (its rigor: block, the project layer) and never
lower it, so a request below the resolved mode changes nothing and the
preview says so rather than quoting a cheaper ceiling than the run would
be held to. The mode is an input to the two terms the tool can compute
and to nothing else: the recipe's stage bound, through the rounds the
mode's own row gives the knobs the checkout leaves unset, and the per-run
cap, through the fraction of the deployed ceiling the mode carries.
That is not the mode budget set --mode takes, which is the accounting
mode (observe or enforce). The output is a ceiling all the same.

That figure is the model ceiling and nothing else: a run also bills for
the machine it asked for, and no budget key bounds compute at all --
the run's own timeout is the cap.
So for every workflow the checkout defines the preview also prints a
compute ceiling -- the workflow's own resources over its own
timeouts.total, at this installation's compute prices -- and says out
loud that it is NOT CAPPED, because for a run whose expensive half is a
render on a big machine the model ceiling is not the worst case. The
basis is timeouts.total and not a render step's own timeout: a render
that overruns still burns the run's clock to the deadline. Without a
price table for the installation's region the line names what is
missing and prints no dollar figure, rather than $0.00.

When the repository's recorded runs of the last 30 days are at least 5,
the preview also prints, clearly labelled typical:, what one run of the
recipe usually costs: the mean recorded cost of each stage kind (on the
model the checkout pins for it, with the recipe's role mapping applied as
a run applies it), at the recipe's typical stage count -- one round of
each loop the recipe and its round knobs leave in, the two fix stages
sharing one mean -- over the runs of the window, whatever they ended as:
a stage counts once it recorded a cost. A kind the window has no cost
for on that model leaves the line out and names the model, rather than
pricing the pinned model with what another one cost. Runs the figure
cannot use are said to be left out, never counted as runs that cost
nothing: a run whose model_usd was a subscription's rather than a bill
(agent.auth oauth, or a cascade run the plan served in full), a
result.json that is missing or unreadable, and a record with no
per-stage cost at all (one from before the runner kept it, or
stages that all cost nothing).

The recipe resolves as it does for a run: the repository's
.fugaro/recipes, the project's published recipes, then the catalog. The
knobs come from the checkout's fugaro.yaml; without a checkout of the
repository here, agent.max_budget_usd is unknown and only
budget.per_run_usd bounds the figure, so with neither the preview says it
is unbounded.

It reads the database's caps and today's counters (the Viewer role), and
the repository's runs (the runs bucket, for the typical line). A recipe
that is not in the checkout also reads the project's recipes from the
runs bucket, as recipes ls does, which a plain project Viewer cannot
read (the converge removes that access): not reading it costs the project layer,
and the ceiling with it. The typical line's own read of the bucket is
the one that costs the line and nothing else: a bucket it cannot read
leaves the ceiling standing. It writes nothing.

Usage: `fugaro budget preview --recipe NAME --runs N [--repo R] [--mode MODE]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for preview |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--mode` | string | "" | no | the rigor mode to preview: poc, startup, pro, critical, hotfix; it may raise the mode the repository resolves (its rigor: block, the project layer) and never lower it, so a mode below the resolved one changes nothing. This is the rigor mode, not the accounting mode budget set --mode takes (observe or enforce) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--recipe` | string | "" | yes | the recipe to preview (ab-judge, default, escalate, lint-fix, pick, premium, rebase, review-only, run-digest, solo, standard, test-and-fix) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | the repository (owner/name, or a path inside its checkout); default: the checkout's origin |
| `--runs` | int | `0` | yes | how many runs to estimate |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro budget resume`

Clear a kill switch (budget admins)

Clear the project's kill switch (--all), one repository's (--repo [owner/name])
or one workspace's (--workspace <name>), recording who and when. --repo with
no value means the repository this checkout belongs to, as it does for set.
Runs start spending again, so nothing is asked for it and a coding agent's
session is refused, exactly as a raise is (D1542). A workspace is named by
its own name alone and takes neither of the other scopes.

| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

| `--workspace` | string | "" | no | one workspace, named as its own project is; its own service's stop flag, in the workspace's own database, so the project it names has to declare one (workspace_members) |

## `fugaro budget set`

Set a cap, the lease limit or the mode (budget admins)

Set caps in the project's budget database, with an ETag-guarded write that shows
the old and the new value.

  --global            the project's daily and per-run caps; also takes --max-reserve and --mode
  --defaults          the caps of every repository that has none of its own
  --repo [owner/name] one repository's caps; --repo with no value means the
                      repository this checkout belongs to, which needs no
                      owner/name at all

--max-reserve (the largest single lease) and --mode (observe, or enforce: caps
bite) are project-wide, so they go with --global. Amounts are US dollars from 0
to 100000, and a per-run cap may not exceed the daily cap of the same scope.
--clear removes the scope's caps.

--repo owner/name always works, from anywhere; the bare --repo is refused
outside a checkout whose origin names a repository, and never stands for the
project-wide caps. kill and resume take --repo the same way. preview needs no
bare form: left out, --repo already means this checkout's repository. show is
the one whose empty --repo is not the checkout (it means no repository
filter), so it takes owner/name.

Raising a cap (setting one that was unset counts), or lowering the mode to
observe, loosens what runs may spend: nothing is asked for it, and a coding
agent's session is refused with the command to run yourself — a raise is the
owner's own step (D1542). --ask puts the question back where you can answer
it. Tightening a cap asks nothing either.

Usage: `fugaro budget set (--global | --defaults | --repo [owner/name]) [--daily USD] [--per-run USD] [--max-reserve USD] [--mode observe|enforce] | --clear`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--ask` | bool | `false` | no | ask before a raise, at a terminal that can answer |
| `--clear` | bool | `false` | no | remove the scope's caps |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--daily` | float64 | `0` | no | the daily cap, in US dollars |
| `--defaults` | bool | `false` | no | the default caps of repositories without their own |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `--global` | bool | `false` | no | the project's own caps |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for set |
| `--max-reserve` | float64 | `0` | no | the largest single lease, in US dollars (with --global) |
| `--mode` | string | "" | no | observe or enforce (with --global) |
| `--per-run` | float64 | `0` | no | the per-run cap, in US dollars |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | one repository's caps, given as owner/name or a path inside its checkout (no value: this checkout's origin) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | accepted and ignored: this command asks nothing |

## `fugaro budget show`

Show caps, today's counters, kill switches, headroom and the runs in flight

Show the project's budget: the mode, the caps, today's (UTC) counted, spent and
notional dollars, the headroom under the caps, the kill switches and the runs
in flight. By default the global figures and the project config's
repositories; --repo one repository; --all every repository the database
knows. Notional is a subscription's list-price figure, never billed and never
capped. Counted is spent plus what runs have reserved and not released; --json
carries that difference as leased_usd, the money leased and not yet spent: a
crashed run's lease is never released, so it stays in the figure for the rest
of the day. --compute adds each repository's compute dollars, read from the
runs bucket: a run's compute is in its own record and nowhere in the
database, so the flag costs a listing of the bucket's repositories and, for
each repository shown, a listing of its runs minted since the previous day
began plus a read of every one of those records (a run's start day is only
known once its record is read), and everything that only needs the counters
leaves it off. The figure is an estimate by design, priced from each run's
own price table, and covers the runs that started today and recorded a
result: a run still in flight has recorded none, so today's is partial, and
a repository whose runs recorded no estimate is null, never 0.

Usage: `fugaro budget show`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--all` | bool | `false` | no | every repository in the database |
| `--compute` | bool | `false` | no | also read each repository's compute dollars from the runs bucket (an estimate; null and n/a where the day's runs recorded none) |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for show |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | only this repository (owner/name, or a path inside its checkout) |

## `fugaro cancel`

Cancel a run, letting the runner open a draft PR first

Cancel RUN (a full run ID, or <repo-slug>/<run-id>).

cancel is the one command that acts on a run and takes no ending. Given the
last four or more characters of a run ID it cancels nothing: it looks them up
among the active runs, lists each one it names as <repo-slug>/<run-id> to
paste, and exits with an error.

cancel writes the run's cancel marker; the runner sees it, stops the current
stage and finalizes a draft PR. If the execution is still in a stage after
--grace, cancel stops it through Cloud Run. It never stops a run that is
opening its PR (finalize) or writing back its cache: it waits up to 10 more
minutes for finalize, and counts writeback as finalized. --grace is never
shorter than the workflow's timeouts.finalize_reserve (5m when neither the run
nor this checkout tells) plus 40s for the runner to notice the cancel. --now
stops the execution at once (so it takes no --grace), without waiting for the
draft PR, but still not mid-finalize.

Usage: `fugaro cancel RUN`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `--grace` | duration | `3m0s` | no | how long to wait for the runner to finalize before cancelling the execution (at least the run's finalize reserve plus 40s) |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for cancel |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print the result as JSON |
| `--now` | bool | `false` | no | cancel the execution at once, without waiting for a draft PR |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

This script depends on the 'bash-completion' package.

	source <(fugaro completion bash)

To load completions for every new session, execute once:

	fugaro completion bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/fugaro

#### macOS:

	fugaro completion bash > $(brew --prefix)/etc/bash_completion.d/fugaro

You will need to start a new shell for this setup to take effect.

Write the minimal fugaro.yaml of a repository whose project publishes a project layer

Write the minimal fugaro.yaml (version, project, gcp_project) into this checkout, for a project that
publishes a project layer. Non-interactive: without --yes it prints the file and exits 1 (a dry run),
writing nothing. It never overwrites a fugaro.yaml, and writes nothing that does not resolve against
the project layer. Unlike fugaro config publish, it never refuses in a coding-agent session: it writes
a repository file, which still goes through a reviewed pull request, not a published, trusted object.

## `fugaro config list`

List the Fugaro installations this machine has

List the project configs under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects (else
~/.config/fugaro/projects), with the GCP project and region of each, what
is known about its published shared config, and the checkouts of its
repositories this machine remembers.

The checkouts are remembered by the commands that run in one and are
not reads the desktop console spawns (fugaro update --repo, fugaro run,
fugaro validate, fugaro backends and the rest of them), in a machine-local
state file beside the project configs. The commands the console's spawn
allow-list covers never record: fugaro doctor and fugaro accounts ls
resolve a checkout too, but a read writes nothing, whoever runs it — the
command cannot tell who spawned it. Every path is re-validated on this
read: a path that
was moved or deleted, that is no longer a git checkout, or whose
fugaro.yaml no longer names this project and this repository is reported
with "valid": false and a reason, and is never silently dropped. The
paths are local state: they are never published to the runs bucket, to
the shared config or to any log.

This is a local read: it opens no bucket and needs no project selected, so it
works outside a checkout and with no config at all (an empty list).

Usage: `fugaro config list`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for list |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro coordinator`

The coordinator's project view: what is in flight, and what collides

The coordinator's deterministic half (docs/coordinator/implementation-plan.md).
Nothing here holds a model credential, a service of its own or a store of its
own: these commands read what fugaro already reads.

Advisory, never authoritative: a collision is reported and never blocks,
reorders or refuses a merge (spec §3).

Usage: `fugaro coordinator`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for coordinator |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro coordinator intents` -- Show what the fleet has declared
- `fugaro coordinator login` -- Sign in to the installation's front door and keep the token in your keychain
- `fugaro coordinator logout` -- Delete the front door credential this project's keychain holds
- `fugaro coordinator report` -- Declare the work you are about to start
- `fugaro coordinator roadmap` -- Change the project's roadmap record, through the installation's front door
- `fugaro coordinator show` -- Show one pull request as the host has it
- `fugaro coordinator status` -- Show the work in flight, and where it collides

## `fugaro coordinator intents`

Show what the fleet has declared

Print every intent record the project's database holds under a repository's
node: the declarations the fleet has made — the branch and the target release
each caller is about to work on, and the files and services it is about to
touch — newest first.

One repository by default, every repository the local config lists with --all,
which prints one list per repository and compares nothing across them: a
branch or a path is a name in one tree.

The records are the ones `coordinator report` and every launch's own declarer
write (P4), and this read takes nothing back: it reports what is stored and
issues no advice, which is the coordinator's whole posture (spec §3).

The read is the caller's own database read, on the project's budget.rtdb_url
database, and what admits it is roles/firebasedatabase.viewer, the role
launchers and operators hold. It opens NO host: no App ID, no App key and no
Bitbucket credential, so a repository on a host the project-wide read refuses
is read here like any other, and with FUGARO_CREDENTIALS_SERVICE_URL set the
command still succeeds where `coordinator status` refuses.
A repository the store holds no record for is an empty list and not a failure
— a project whose coordinator is off is read with the same argv — while a
database that refused the read is refused here, exit 1, naming the role: a
console that read a refusal as "nothing declared" would draw a quiet project
where the truth is that nobody could look. A stored record this build cannot
decode is refused the same way, never shown with a field dropped.

declared_by is what whoever declared it wrote about itself, and never an
identity: a run's own launch record, or a person's report. Nothing verifies it
and nothing here authorises anything by it (finding #11). The branch, the
release, the paths and the services are the caller's own text carried as data
(Q14 A): the text output sanitises each one, and an instruction found in any of
them is never acted on.
Exit codes: 1 for a refusal of the caller's own argv or of the database, 2 for
a failure that is not the project's.

With --json the document is printed as it is stored: one repository with
{"repo", "provider", "intents"}, and every intent as the fields its record
carries — id, declared_by, at, branch, release, files and services — and no
others. With --all the repositories are a list under "repos", in the order
the selection names them.

Usage: `fugaro coordinator intents`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--all` | bool | `false` | no | read every repository the local config lists, one list each |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for intents |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | the repository to read (owner/name; default: the local config's, when it lists one) |
| `--since` | string | `0` | no | only declarations made within this long (36h, 90m, 7d; 0 for every declaration the store holds, which is the default) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro coordinator login`

Sign in to the installation's front door and keep the token in your keychain

Run the authorization-code flow this installation's front door serves
(docs/coordinator/implementation-plan.md, P9f; the flow is the MCP server
plan's M5): a loopback redirect with PKCE, so nothing the browser carries
back can be replayed from a history, a log or a shoulder.

The front door's URL is read from the installation's own outputs, which is
the only place it is published: Cloud Run's URL carries the project number
and nothing derives it. An installation whose front door is off publishes
none, and that is this command's refusal.

The refresh token it receives is stored in the operating system's keychain,
under an item named after the project, and never in a file. `fugaro
coordinator logout` deletes it. What the command prints is the issuer and
the scopes: never the token, the code or the verifier.

The scope defaults to roadmap:write, which is what the roadmap group's
commands hold. It is an operator's scope on this installation's own list:
a person who is not an operator is refused by the door, at the approval
step, where the list is read.
Exit codes: 1 for a refusal (no front door, no scope this build mints,
the person's own refusal, or an installation that would not store the
token), 2 for a failure of the front door or of the keychain.

Usage: `fugaro coordinator login`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for login |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--scope` | stringArray | `[roadmap:write]` | no | the scope to ask for (repeatable; the front door mints tasks:read, tasks:write, state:read, state:write, roadmap:write) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro coordinator logout`

Delete the front door credential this project's keychain holds

Remove the keychain item `fugaro coordinator login` wrote, which is the
whole of what this machine holds for the front door: the token is in no
file and in no cache, so deleting the item is the end of it.

An item that is not there is not an error: the state a person asks for is
the state they get. The token family itself is not revoked by this command
— the door revokes a family where it is revoked, and a device that lost
its credential is not a theft signal (M5b).
Exit codes: 1 for a refusal, 2 for a keychain that could not be reached.

| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |

| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

## `fugaro coordinator report`

Declare the work you are about to start

Write one intent record for this project's repository: the branch and the
target release the caller declares, and the files and services it is about
to touch, so that work still in flight can be seen before code exists
(spec §6).

The record's ID is derived from the caller and the declaration, and from
nothing else: reporting the same declaration twice writes ONE document, and
the second report replaces the first rather than adding to it.

The caller is who the local config names (user:), else git config
user.email, and a report nobody can be named for is refused: every record
is somebody's declaration, and one nobody can be named for is not one. That
name is a declaration too — nothing verifies it, and nothing authorises
anything by it (finding #11).

This command writes and reads nothing back: it prints the record it wrote
and issues no advice, which is the coordinator's whole posture in v1
(spec §3, advisory and never authoritative).

The write goes through the caller's own credentials, on the project's
budget.rtdb_url database. The rules grant /coordinator a read and no write
to anyone, so the write is admitted by the database role its caller holds
(roles/firebasedatabase.admin, which terraform.budget_admins have); a
launcher who is not an admin reports through the coordinator's front door
once it is deployed.

Usage: `fugaro coordinator report`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--branch` | string | "" | no | the branch you are about to work on |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--file` | stringArray | `[]` | no | a path you are about to touch (repeatable) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for report |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print the record as it was written |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--release` | string | "" | no | the target release (default: the one the branch names, e.g. release/v0.11.0) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | the repository this report is about (owner/name; default: the local config's, when it lists one) |
| `--service` | stringArray | `[]` | no | a service you are about to touch (repeatable) |

## `fugaro coordinator roadmap`

Change the project's roadmap record, through the installation's front door

The commands that change the project's roadmap record
(docs/coordinator/implementation-plan.md, P9f).

Every one of them is one call to a tool the installation's front door
serves, over the credential `fugaro coordinator login` left in your
keychain. The front door queues the change and a job applies it as the
coordinator's own account: these commands hold no database credential and
write no node, so nothing here can reach the record directly.

Each write prints the request's id and then waits up to a minute for the
record's answer. A change that has not been applied by then is still
queued: read it later with `fugaro coordinator roadmap request <id>`.

The scope the tools need (roadmap:write) is an operator's on this
installation's own list, so a person who is not an operator is refused by
the door.
Exit codes: 1 for a refusal (no credential, no front door, a write the
record refused, a tool the token may not call), 2 for a failure of the
front door or of the record.

Usage: `fugaro coordinator roadmap`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for roadmap |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro coordinator roadmap need` -- Record that one task needs another
- `fugaro coordinator roadmap publish` -- Put a checkout's plan graphs into the roadmap record
- `fugaro coordinator roadmap releases` -- Write a stream's releases
- `fugaro coordinator roadmap request` -- Read back what happened to a roadmap request
- `fugaro coordinator roadmap unneed` -- Remove a recorded dependency between two tasks
- `fugaro coordinator roadmap unpublish` -- Remove a published plan from the record

## `fugaro coordinator roadmap need`

Record that one task needs another

Record a dependency between two tasks, across plans or streams
(roadmap_need, D2112).

A reason is required and not decoration: an edge nobody can check is not
one, and the reason is what a reviewer reads when the record is read.
The dependency is one the coordinator reports and never one it enforces:
nothing here blocks a merge, a run or a release (spec §3).

## `fugaro coordinator roadmap publish`

Put a checkout's plan graphs into the roadmap record

Publish the graph artifact beside a plan document, from any checkout
(roadmap_publish_plan, D2111).

Read the plan's graph where it sits — `docs/plans/x.md` is described by
`docs/plans/x.graph.json` — and send it, trimmed to what the record holds
and carrying where it came from: this repository, the artifact's path and
the commit HEAD names. A symlink anywhere on the way to the file, a file
that is not a regular file, and a graph this build refuses all end the run
before anything is sent; an artifact with uncommitted changes is refused
too, because what is published is what is committed.

`--expect` is the version of the plan document you last read, and the
record compares it with the version it holds: an empty `--expect` is the
claim that the record holds no such plan, so leave it out for a plan the
record does not hold and send what the record holds for one it does. A
publish that carries the version it read and sends the same artifact
writes nothing the second time — the record compares the document it holds
with the one it is sent — and one that carries a version the record has
moved past is refused, which is what keeps two people publishing one plan
from two checkouts from overwriting each other. This command holds no read
that would fetch the version for you: the refusal names it, and sending it
back is the next run.

`--all` publishes every graph artifact under the checkout's docs/, each its
own request. `--releases <file>` imports a release catalogue — this
repository's `docs/release-streams.yaml` is the one that exists — one
release per stream, named by the catalogue. It is a flag a person passes
and never a default: a repository with no such file publishes its plans
the same way.

Nothing is read from the checkout but the artifact, and nothing leaves it
but the trimmed document and its provenance.

Usage: `fugaro coordinator roadmap publish [<plan>]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--all` | bool | `false` | no | publish every graph artifact under the checkout's docs/ |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--expect` | string | "" | no | the version of the plan document you last read; leave it out for a plan the record does not hold |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for publish |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--releases` | string | "" | no | a release catalogue to import, such as docs/release-streams.yaml (never a default) |

## `fugaro coordinator roadmap releases set`

Write one release of a stream

Write one release document: its name, its state, its position and the
version you last read (roadmap_release_set).

**`--expect` is not a formality.** It is the version of the release
document you read before you decided what to write, and the record compares
it with the version it holds now: a release somebody else has changed since
is refused, with the version it holds, rather than written over. For a
release the record does not hold yet, leave it out — the empty string says
"I read nothing, and I expect nothing", which is the one claim that cannot
be stale.
