## `fugaro coordinator roadmap request`

Read back what happened to a roadmap request

Read one roadmap request's outcome: applied, refused with the reason and the
value the record holds now, failed, or still pending (roadmap_request).

The id is the one a write printed. A request belongs to the person who
queued it, and an id that is not yours is answered exactly as one that does
not exist, so this cannot be used to ask what other people have asked for.
This reads once and does not wait: a pending request is a state, not a
failure, and running the command again is how you look later.

## `fugaro coordinator show`

Show one pull request as the host has it

One pull request as the host has it, whole: the number, the address, the
title, the description, the state, the draft flag, the source branch and the
branch it targets, and the author's account id, each exactly as the host
answered it.

The description is why this read exists: the stored view carries no body — a
body is unbounded text written by whoever opened the pull request, and one
per record would ride in the document every reader of the view fetches — so
a console that draws one reads it here. It is untrusted text, and a renderer
sanitises it before it reaches a line or a cell.

The read is the installation's: one read-only token for the repository,
minted at the project's own published credentials service against the
caller's own Google ID token and carrying the named read-only permission
set — contents, pull requests and metadata, all read (Q3 answered (A)).
This command holds no GitHub App key and no Bitbucket credential, and it
reads no environment variable to find the service: a project that publishes
none is one whose host read is refused (exit 1). No credential of the host's
reaches the output.
A repository on a host this read does not serve is refused the way the
project-wide view refuses it (reconciliation Q12 (A), finding #30): a
bitbucket repository is read through the same service, one repository's read
token at a time, and refused where the project publishes none.

A pull request the host does not have is the host's own failure (exit 2),
carrying the host's status, and never an empty document: an empty one would
draw a pull request with no description, which is a different fact.
Exit codes: 1 for a project with no credentials service (or the refusals
above), 2 for a failure of the host.

With --json the document is printed as it is: number, url, title, body,
state, draft, branch, base and author, every field the host's own answer and
absent when it gave none.

Usage: `fugaro coordinator show`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for show |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--pr` | int | `0` | no | the pull request number |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | the repository the pull request is in (owner/name) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro coordinator status`

Show the work in flight, and where it collides

Join a repository's pull requests with its run records and print the view:
each pull request, the runs behind it, the branch and target release it declares,
the files and services those runs touched, and every pair of work still in
flight that touches the same file or service.

One repository by default, every repository the local config lists with --all,
which prints a view per repository and compares nothing across them: a service
is a path's shape in one tree, so two repositories' paths say nothing about
each other.

The pull requests listed are the ones the runs name, and that is the whole of
the list this reader can produce: gitprov reads one pull request by number and
has no call that lists a repository's (finding #10), so a pull request no run
names is never asked for. The rule the join is written to — a pull request no
run names is listed as having none, because it is work somebody has open and
dropping it is the one thing this view must not do — is not reached by this
command today.

Every repository is read through the installation's credentials service: one
read-only token for that repository, minted there against the caller's own
Google ID token and carrying the service's person read permission set —
contents, pull requests and metadata, all read (Q3 answered (A)) — and
cached for the token's life, so a second read of the same repository mints
nothing.
The service's URL is the project's own published credentials_service block and
never an environment variable, and this command holds no GitHub App key at
all: an installation that publishes no service is one whose host read is
refused (exit 1) rather than made with a key a person's machine does not hold,
and --from-store is the view to read instead.
Exit codes: 1 for a project with no credentials service (or the refusals
above), 2 for a failure of the host.
A bitbucket repository is read through the same service, one repository's read
token at a time, and refused where the project publishes none
(reconciliation Q12 (A), finding #30).

--from-store is a different read of the same view (D364): it prints what the
sweep already stored, coordinator/repos/<slug>/ in the project's database,
through the caller's own credentials — roles/firebasedatabase.viewer is what
admits it — and with the same --repo and --all selection as above. It opens no
host and holds no App ID, no App key and no Bitbucket credential: everything a
stored view says about a pull request is what the sweep read once. It is the
read a console makes, and it needs no credentials service and no host read at
all — it works on a project whose installation publishes none.
With --json, one repository is printed as it is stored: {"repo":
"owner/name", "stored": true, "view": {the view document}, "stale": {the
sweep's marker, as stored}}. A repository the coordinator has never
reconciled is "stored": false, and the document then holds the runs half of
the view — the runs bucket alone, with the pull requests those runs name
listed and no host state for them — so a console reads a project whose
coordinator is off with the same argv. --since bounds that half, and a
stored view is printed as the sweep wrote it. What decides between the two
is the database and never the local config: a teammate's config is the
published shared one, and it does not carry the coordinator's switch at all.
The stale marker is printed exactly as stored, with no age computed from it:
the stored view carries no time by design (internal/coordinator/sweep.go).

The launcher of a run is printed as what it is — the string the run's own launch
record wrote about itself — and never as an identity.

This command writes nothing of its own: no service, no model credential, and no
store it maintains. Without --from-store it reads nothing of the coordinator's
either — it is the read the CLI already performs, the runs bucket and a pull
request read that can only read — while --from-store reads the view the sweep
stored and nothing else.

Usage: `fugaro coordinator status`

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--all` | bool | `false` | no | read every repository the local config lists, one view each |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--from-store` | bool | `false` | no | print the view the sweep stored, with no host read and no key (falls back to the runs alone when none is stored) |

## `fugaro craft`

Show the model and the credential or pool each craft runs on

Show the four crafts: the coder, the first-line review, the senior review
and the security review.

Each craft runs a model and sends its calls out on a credential or a pool, and
the two halves inherit separately: the first-line review follows the coder and
the security review follows the senior review, so a craft that sets only one
half keeps the other half it follows. A craft that sets no access anywhere
resolves to the project's default credential.

Every half names where it came from: the layer that wrote it (repo, local or
project), the craft it was inherited from, or default when nothing set it. A
pool holding two or more Claude OAuth credentials serves nothing until the
project's subscription-spread switch is on, and the row says so.

The read is offline: it reads this checkout's fugaro.yaml, the installation's
own config and the project layer file the last cloud read cached, and reaches
no bucket, no database and no host.

## `fugaro creds ls`

List the credentials the bundle secret holds: names and metadata, never a value (the owner)

List the credentials the credentials service's bundle secret holds: one row
per credential in the document, with its NAME, whether it is PRESENT, and the
document's last-changed time (the container's newest version metadata).

NAME is the name in the document's own spelling — the name fugaro creds set
takes. A named Claude account's row is claude-oauth-token-<account>, where <account>
is the account the policy's accounts block speaks.

Nothing else is printed: never a value, never a prefix of one, never a length
that would narrow a guess. --json carries the same shape.

The listing needs the container to exist, and it needs its newest version to be
one the service could read: an absent container, a container with no version, an
unreadable payload, a document the service's own loader refuses, and a version
that is DISABLED are each a named failure, never an empty list — a listing that
answered nothing for any of them would read as "the bundle holds no credential"
while the service is in fact issuing from one this command could not read.

It is refused from a coding agent's session and from a run's process, before
anything is read.

## `fugaro creds set`

Set or replace one credential in the credentials service's bundle secret (the owner)

Set or replace one credential in the credentials service's bundle, the ONE
Secret Manager secret the service reads (Q6). The bundle is a YAML document
whose keys are credential names and whose values are the credentials; this
command reads it, sets or replaces the entry NAME and writes it back as a new
version, and then disables the version it replaced.

NAME is a credential the service can issue, in the document's own spelling:

  claude-oauth-token                    the default Claude account's OAuth token (tier A)
  claude-oauth-token-<account>       a named Claude account's OAuth token (tier A)
  anthropic-api-key                the project's Anthropic API key (tier B)
  github-app-key                  the GitHub App's private key (no tier: the mint signs with it)
  bitbucket-token                   the upstream Bitbucket token (no tier: the git proxy issues this entry for the repositories the published node admits with proxy: true, and every other Bitbucket run's job still uses its own mounted copy until the flip)
  bitbucket-read-consumer             the Bitbucket read consumer (no tier: the service's read mint exchanges it for a read-scoped token): a YAML mapping of key, secret and workspace, one field per line, so redirect it from a file — the hidden prompt takes one line
  provider-key                 the project's provider credential (tier C: the service's provider route authenticates upstream with it): a YAML mapping of key, base_url and auth, one field per line, so redirect it from a file — the hidden prompt takes one line. It is read by a credentials service from 0.22.0 on: where the service that serves the bundle is older, this write is refused and `fugaro update` is the one command that moves it
  claude-oauth-token--review-signing  the default account's review-signing key (no tier: the service's sign
                                     route computes a MAC with it; written by --generate below)
  claude-oauth-token-<account>--review-signing     a named account's review-signing key (no tier, and --generate's NAME too)

The value is read only from stdin: pipe or redirect it in
(fugaro creds set claude-oauth-token < token-file), or, when stdin is a terminal, paste it
at a hidden prompt. It is never taken from an argument, a flag or the
environment, and never printed. --generate changes WHERE the bytes come from
and nothing else: they are drawn in this process, and they are never printed
either. One trailing newline (\n or \r\n) is dropped, and the command says so.
A value must be 4 bytes to 8192, on one line, with
no whitespace at either end; a longer value is a document the service's loader
would refuse, so it is refused here instead.

--generate writes a review-signing key and takes no value of its own
(--generate=anything is a malformed flag): a review-signing key is an HMAC key
with no upstream to paste one from, so this process draws 32 bytes from
crypto/rand and writes them into the bundle. Every other NAME is refused: an
account's review-signing names are the only ones it takes, and the rotation
window's own entry is not one of them — asked to write it, the command refuses,
because it writes the current entry and derives the window's from it.

Two runs ROTATE the key. The first writes a fresh value where the entry was;
the second writes a fresh one again and carries the value it replaced, byte for
byte, under the same name with -previous appended. The service signs with
the current entry and verifies against the current and the previous one, and
against nothing older, so there is no instant in which it holds neither.

Two consecutive generates REVOKE the key that was current before the first of
them: the second run's window holds the first run's key, and the original is in
neither entry, so a signature made with it stops verifying. It is not escrowed
and it is not re-signable, and the honest remedy is a re-review of the head.

github-app-key is the ONE multi-line entry: it is an RSA private key in a PEM,
so it has to come in on stdin, from the key file the App's page downloads
(fugaro creds set github-app-key < PATH-TO-THE-KEY-FILE) — the hidden prompt reads one
line and cannot take a paste of a whole key, so it refuses this name and says
so. The value must be exactly one PEM block, its -----BEGIN line to its
matching -----END line and nothing else, and it must be a key the service's
mint can parse (internal/gitprov/github's ParsePrivateKey: PKCS#1 "RSA PRIVATE
KEY" or PKCS#8 "PRIVATE KEY", RSA). A single line of anything, a PEM with a
line of text around it, and a key the mint cannot use are each refused before
the write, and no refusal repeats a byte of the value.

The write is a read-modify-write of one document: the other entries keep their
bytes, and the whole document is parsed with the service's own loader
(internal/credsvc) before it is written, so what this command stores is what
the service accepts. After the write the bundle is read back and compared: if
it is not the document this command wrote, another write landed underneath and
this one lost it, which is said plainly and exits non-zero. Nothing is retried
silently.

A verified write then DISABLES the version it replaced, which the output names:
a rotated-away bundle that stays enabled keeps every superseded credential
readable by anyone who can read the container, which is the one thing a
rotation is for. Terraform cannot do this (it creates the container and manages
no version), so the command that writes a version retires the one before it. A
disable that fails is reported on stderr and does not fail the command: the new
credential is live either way.

The command needs the container to exist — the installation's Terraform creates
it (Task C1.18) and no command of ours does — and it works with the owner's own
project IAM (Project Owner or Editor: secretmanager.versions.get, .add and
.disable). There is no service account, no actAs and no operator grant on this
container: a secretVersionAdder on it is the ability to read every credential
in the bundle at once.

It is refused from a coding agent's session and from a run's process, before
anything is read, and it is never covered by --yes: there is no non-interactive
form.

Usage: `fugaro creds set NAME`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `--generate` | bool | `false` | no | generate a fresh review-signing key instead of reading a value (the review-signing names only) |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for set |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

## `fugaro doctor`

Check that Fugaro is set up and ready, without changing anything

doctor only ever reads: the environment, Terraform, the local project config
and its installation's billing and IAM policy (with a budget backend, who can
sign sign-in tokens for it: warnings, never changes), the Fugaro plugin's wiring in
.claude/settings.json, a checkout's fugaro.yaml and its stored secrets by
name. With --check-github-app, in your own terminal, it also asks GitHub whether
each GitHub App the config records is installed on its repository with the
permissions Fugaro's runs ask for: that is the one thing that reads a secret's
value (the App's private key, with your own credentials, held in memory only to
sign, never printed), and it is refused in a coding agent's session. With
--check-bitbucket-token, in your own terminal, it also reads the credentials
service's bundle to see that it holds a Bitbucket token and asks Bitbucket
whether it still accepts it, one GET /repositories/<repo> per proxied
repository: that too reads a secret's value (with your own credentials, in
memory only, never printed) and is refused in a coding agent's session.
Otherwise it never prints a secret's value and never creates, enables or
changes anything.

Inside a checkout whose project publishes a project layer (fugaro config
publish), doctor also names which layer applies, flags a run that launched
without it or on an older generation, a stale per-repository copy (the one
Cloud Build and the daily image check read), and an image that is not the one
the checkout resolves to now: a workflow whose image was last built from
settings it no longer resolves to, and, for a workflow whose image is the
project's catalog's own entry, an entry no build has built or one whose
definition moved (fugaro image build <entry>). None of these fails when the
bucket is unreachable: the layer line falls back to the offline cache and says
so, and a bucket read that does not answer leaves its image line out instead
of failing the command.

--plugin checks only the plugin's wiring: offline, no credentials, safe for
CI. --strict makes a stale, unpinned or foreign plugin fail the command. A
checkout that never opted in to the pin is informational rather than a
failure, because nothing in the tree writes a pin any more and that checkout is
the normal one; "cannot compare" — a development build, an unreadable install
record — is informational too. "not installed" is a warning, because the
plugin on this machine is what carries the skills. A repository's CI runs
fugaro doctor --plugin --strict; with --strict the install on the machine is
not evaluated at all, because a runner has no Claude Code.

--offline checks the update class and nothing else, and it makes no cloud call,
no network call and no secret read: the plugin's wiring and the install on this
machine, the login unit that runs the orchestrator daemon, and the base image
this checkout resolves to where a local installation is configured to answer
it. Every check whose answer lives in the project's Realtime Database or the
runs bucket — the published policy, the deployed rules, and whether a
workflow's job was built from the image settings it resolves to now — and the
one that asks whether a newer release is available, is skipped rather than
guessed: it comes back with skipped true and ok false, and
a problem saying what could not be read, and it fails nothing, with or without
--strict. A reader of --json should take ok true as "checked and fine" and
skipped true as "not checked"; that pair is the whole contract. It is the
check the Fugaro skills run at the start of a session.

With no local Fugaro installation configured, doctor says so and names
fugaro setup as the fix, rather than guessing at a project.

What doctor prints is a verdict and then only what to do: one sentence and one
fix per item, each item fugaro update puts right ending in that command.
--all prints every check, the informational lines included, and --security the
IAM and security sweep (who can read a stored credential, who can sign a
budget token, what a launcher may start). The default view never hides a
security finding that is a warning, and it says how many findings it left out
when it leaves any out. Every check, with its full text, is in --json whatever
the flags.

Exit 1 when a check fails, with the one-line fix to run.

Usage: `fugaro doctor [--json] [--all] [--security] [--plugin] [--strict] [--offline]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--all` | bool | `false` | no | print every check, the informational and audit lines included |
| `--check-bitbucket-token` | bool | `false` | no | also check the credentials service's bundle holds a Bitbucket token and that Bitbucket still accepts it: reads the bundle with your own credentials, in memory only, for one GET /repositories/<repo> per proxied repository (refused in a coding agent's session; GODEBUG=http2debug would print the token, so unset it) |
| `--check-github-app` | bool | `false` | no | also check each recorded GitHub App is installed with the permissions runs ask for: reads the App's private key from Secret Manager with your own credentials, in memory only, for one signed token (refused in a coding agent's session; GODEBUG=http2debug would print the token, so unset it) |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--dir` | string | `.` | no | a directory in the checkout, for the plugin wiring |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for doctor |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--offline` | bool | `false` | no | check the update class's local checks and record a skip for each check that needs a credential or the network: no cloud call, no network call, no secret read (the session-start check the skills run) |
| `--plugin` | bool | `false` | no | check only the plugin's wiring (offline, no credentials) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--security` | bool | `false` | no | also print the IAM and security sweep (who may read a credential, who may sign a budget token, what a launcher may start) |
| `--strict` | bool | `false` | no | fail on a stale, unpinned or foreign plugin (CI mode); an un-wired checkout is information, not a failure |

## `fugaro estimate`

Reprice one run's recorded tokens on another model

Reprice one run on another model: the token counts the run recorded, priced
at the named model's list rates. Nothing is run and nothing is written.

The figure is an ESTIMATE and not the run's bill: it reprices the recorded
tokens and nothing else, so what a repricing cannot reproduce is left out.
A call that passed a long-context tier was priced per call, web searches are
priced apart from the tokens, and a charge settled from a reservation, one
recorded as unreconciled and a call whose usage could not be read are not in
the counts at all. The estimate assumes the run would have taken the same
cache ratio.

The run is named with --run, or found the way `runs ls --pr` finds one: --pr N
over one repository (--repo, or the local config's only one) and the last
90d unless --since says otherwise. A pull request with several runs is not
one figure: they are listed, and one is named with --run.

The model is a row of the price table this project prices runs from -- the
built-in catalog, with the owner's model_prices over it -- named by its exact
ID or one of that row's aliases: no prefixes, and no guess at what a nickname
meant. A model the table has no row for is refused with the IDs it has. The
date of the table the figure was priced from is printed beside it, and a
table past its own check window warns.

A run whose record carries no per-model token counts -- one that never
finalized, or one that finalized before this binary recorded them -- is
refused: there is nothing to reprice, and no total is estimated in its place.

Usage: `fugaro estimate`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for estimate |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--model` | string | "" | no | the model to price the run's tokens at (a price table model ID) |
| `--pr` | int | `0` | no | the pull request whose run to reprice (needs one repository) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | the repository a --pr lookup reads (owner/name, or a path inside its checkout) |
| `--run` | string | "" | no | the run to reprice (<run-id>, <slug>/<run-id>, or an ending) |
| `--since` | string | `90d` | no | with --pr, only runs started within this long (90d, 36h, 90m; 0 for all) |

## `fugaro followups`

File the findings a merged run deferred as follow-up tasks

File the review findings RUN deferred as tasks of their own, one per group the
triage tied together and one per finding when it tied none.

The parent pull request has to be merged: a deferral is work the review left
behind on purpose, and the merge is what says so. The pull request is found on
the code host by the branch the run's launcher wrote -- fugaro/<run id> for a
first run, the branch its task carries for a follow-up -- and never by a number
the run's record names, because the record is written by the job: a job that
could name somebody else's merged pull request would have this command file
tasks from its own text (F30).

By default the plan is printed and nothing is written. --launch files them,
at most --max of them (10 by default), as debt tasks: each carries the parent
run and the finding keys it settles (follow_up_of), the debt mark
(fugaro runs ls --debt), and the mode the parent's own record resolved, which
the run re-resolves through its floors -- never a recorded hotfix, which is an
operator's own run and not a task's (D1844). The finding text and the triage's
reason are fenced and indented as data in the brief.

A group a run already covers is skipped, found through the run list, so a
second call files only what is left and an interrupted one can simply be run
again.

Usage: `fugaro followups RUN`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for followups |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--launch` | bool | `false` | no | launch the tasks this call plans; without it the plan is printed and nothing is written |
| `--max` | int | `10` | no | file at most N tasks in this call |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

## `fugaro graph`

Print the project's dependency graph

Print the project's dependency graph as one versioned document.
Every scope is read from the project's database through the caller's own
credential: the coordinator's stored view is what the coordinator's sweep
already wrote, so this command opens no host and works in a directory that
is not a checkout. The one fact it needs is each repository's git
provider, which the project config's repos entries carry and which the
repository's slug is keyed by: a repository whose entry leaves provider
out is refused with the sentence that says where to set it, rather than
graphed from a guess.

--source selects the scope, and the set is closed. all (the default) is
every scope that exists: the coordinator's stored view and one scope per
orchestrator this installation has. coordinator is that view alone;
orchestrator:<id> is one orchestrator's node under /orchestrator, its work
items as nodes and their depends_on as edges; local:<id> is the same node
read as one this machine's daemon drives, falling back to the daemon's
cached brief when the node cannot be read. An id is one lower-case letter or
digit, then up to 39 more of those or a hyphen, and nothing else: anything
that does not match is refused before anything is read, and so is an id the
project's database does not hold, with a sentence naming it and pointing at
fugaro orchestrator ls. Which ids exist is what that listing asks — a key
under /orchestrator — and not whether a state node was written, so an id it
lists is a scope even with no state yet: a daemon that has beaten its lease
and saved none is down rather than refused. A local:<id> is refused when this
machine holds no cached brief for it and there is no node to read, because
the cache stands in for the local scope alone: an orchestrator:<id> the
database does not hold is refused even on a machine holding a brief for it.

The coordinator's scope is every repository the local config lists, and a
repository the sweep has never reconciled is read as its runs alone — the
half of the view that needs no credential — rather than dropped. Which
half it is is a fact about the repository and not about the scope: the
scope's state is down when the project lists repositories and the sweep
has stored a view for none of them, and up once it has stored one, beside
records that may still be the runs half.

With --json the document is printed as the console reads it: its version,
when it was assembled, one entry per scope in sources, the nodes, the edges
(the coordinator's view has none; an orchestrator's are its work items'
depends_on) and the warnings. Without it, a short table: each scope's state,
then its nodes grouped by release, then the edges.

--watch --json prints a whole document per change instead of one and
exits, one compact object per line: the first snapshot at once, then one
document for every change of the scopes it covers, at most one a second,
and a document every 30 seconds while nothing changes. Every document
carries the stream's own id and a sequence that rises within it, so a
reader reads a new id as a whole new snapshot rather than comparing its
sequence with the one before. It subscribes once per scope subtree — the
coordinator's and the orchestrator's for all, or the one node a named
orchestrator scope reads — and a scope it cannot reach is a state in the
document rather than an exit. A local scope falls back to the daemon's
cached brief, which the stream re-reads on every document it writes.
--watch needs --json, which is the only shape a reader of the stream can
consume.

Exit codes: 1 for a refused scope or a project with no database, 2 for a
failure of the database or the runs bucket.

Usage: `fugaro graph`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for graph |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print the graph document as JSON |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--source` | string | `all` | no | the scope to read: all, coordinator, orchestrator:<id> or local:<id> |
| `--watch` | bool | `false` | no | print a whole document per change, one compact object per line (needs --json) |

## `fugaro image add`

Add an image catalog entry to this machine's project config

Add a named image to the project's image catalog, in this machine's project
config: the copy fugaro update publishes to the project's policy node
(image_catalog). The entry's source is a Dockerfile in one of the project's
repositories (--dockerfile owner/name:path, with --branch), a Dockerfile
written out here (--inline <file>), or an image that already exists
(--image <ref>), and its tags are what a repository's needs: is matched
against. The three are one entry's alternatives and are refused together
rather than resolved.

Nothing is built and nothing is published here: fugaro image build <name>
builds the entry's image, and fugaro update publishes the catalog. --default
marks the entry a job whose repositories name no needs runs; a catalog marks
one entry, or none.

## `fugaro image build`

Build a catalog entry's image with Cloud Build, or the workflow's derived image; --local builds the derived one with local Docker

Build an image with Cloud Build.

With an image catalog published (fugaro image ls lists its entries), it
submits the catalog entry you name, or every entry of this checkout's
catalog — one whose Dockerfile is another repository's is passed over.
An entry whose source is a Dockerfile or an inline definition is built:
the definition is copied into the project's bucket, the build reads that
one object, mounts the workflow's secrets as file secrets, smoke-tests
the candidate without network and promotes it into the installation's
shared registry with a content tag naming the definition it built. An
entry whose source is a prebuilt image is not built: its run is the
smoke of that reference against the runtime contract alone, and the
record it writes is what fugaro doctor reads back — --no-smoke has
nothing to leave out of it. Run it from the checkout of the entry's own
repository: the build account, the provider credential and the secrets
are that repository's.

Without a catalog — or with --workflow, which selects the per-workflow
case — Cloud Build builds the workflow's derived image from the
repository's base branch as the repository's build account (cloning with
its bitbucket-token, or a read-only token its GitHub App mints) and
pushes it to the repository's own registry, which fugaro update --repo
creates. It pushes a candidate, smoke-tests it without network, and only
then points latest at it and records what it was built from, unless a
newer build is already recorded. Run it from the repository's checkout:
the checkout's fugaro.yaml and origin say what to build.

A Cloud Build is billable, so it asks nothing: the build's estimated cost
is reserved against the project's budget before it is submitted, the way a
run's is, and a build no cap has room for is refused with the cap, what the
day counts and the one command that raises it (fugaro budget show says what
the project holds). A CLI that died mid-build leaves its reservation open
and the next build gives it back. Pricing an image comes from the Cloud
Billing catalog, and a build whose price cannot be read is submitted
uncounted, after one line that says so.
An installation whose project config sets no budget.rtdb_url has no budget
backend and no lease to take: its builds are submitted uncounted, and
fugaro update --firebase-project in the checkout adds the backend.
--local builds with your own Docker and costs nothing in the cloud.

Usage: `fugaro image build [name]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--base` | string | "" | no | base image (default: for a Cloud Build build the local config's base_images entry for the workflow's base, else the published fugaro-base matching this fugaro version) |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for build |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output (--local only: a Cloud Build reports itself as text) |
| `--local` | bool | `false` | no | build with the local Docker daemon from the checkout you are in |
| `--no-smoke` | bool | `false` | no | skip the smoke test of the built image (on Cloud Build, latest is then promoted unsmoked) |
| `--no-wait` | bool | `false` | no | submit the Cloud Build build and return without waiting for it |
| `--platform` | string | `linux/amd64` | no | image platform; Cloud Run runs linux/amd64 |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | owner/name (or a path inside its checkout) of the repository to build with Cloud Build (default: the checkout's origin, which it must match) |
| `--tag` | string | "" | no | tag for the built image (default fugaro-<dir>-<workflow>:local) |
| `--workflow` | string | "" | no | workflow to build; optional when fugaro.yaml defines one |

## `fugaro image check`

Decide whether each workflow's image needs a rebuild (the daily check; locally it only prints the decision)

Evaluate the rebuild triggers of the repository's workflows against the head of
its base branch: a blobless clone, the build record in the runs bucket, and the
base image's digest.

Run from a checkout, it uses your own git access and ADC and only prints each
workflow's decision: it never submits a build (--dry-run is accepted, and is what
it always does). Start a rebuild with fugaro image build.

With --job, as the repository's daily check job runs it (it refuses to submit
unless CLOUD_RUN_JOB or CLOUD_RUN_EXECUTION is set, as Cloud Run sets them, and
in a coding agent's session; --dry-run is always allowed), it reads the job's
spec from FUGARO_CHECK_SPEC, submits a Cloud Build rebuild when a trigger fires
(not with --dry-run), writes builds/<slug>/<workflow>/check.json, and logs one
JSON line per workflow. It exits 2 when the check itself failed.

With --job --catalog it is the project's catalog check job instead (D1148): one
run of the project's own job, reading its spec from FUGARO_CATALOG_CHECK_SPEC,
deciding every entry of the project's image catalog and submitting at most one
Cloud Build per entry that fires, as that entry's own repository's build account.
It writes builds/<slug>/catalog/<entry>/check.json and logs one JSON line per
entry it decides (an entry a prebuilt image answers has nothing to build).

Usage: `fugaro image check`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--catalog` | bool | `false` | no | with --job: run as the project's catalog check job (reads FUGARO_CATALOG_CHECK_SPEC; submits one rebuild per changed entry) |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--dry-run` | bool | `false` | no | never submit a build (locally the check never does anyway) |
| `--force` | bool | `false` | no | decide rebuild whatever the triggers say (with --job: a build is submitted) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for check |
| `--job` | bool | `false` | no | run as the repository's daily check job (reads FUGARO_CHECK_SPEC; submits rebuilds) |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output (locally; the job always logs JSON) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--workflow` | string | "" | no | check only this workflow |

## `fugaro image ls`

List what this project's image catalog names: each entry's name, the tags it
provides, which one is the default, what it is built from and the digest the
last build of it recorded.

The catalog is the project's; the installation's shared images are a different
inventory, and --shared prints those instead: each image's key, reference and
digest, and the repositories and jobs on it. The two are one command with a
flag, never two ls commands, so there is no question of which one to run.

A project with no catalog of its own lists nothing: fugaro image add writes
an entry, and fugaro update publishes the catalog to the project's policy
node (image_catalog), which is what a job reads.

## `fugaro image map set`

Map a repository to an image catalog entry, in this machine's project config

Map one of the project's repositories to an image catalog entry, in this
machine's project config: the copy fugaro update publishes to the project's
policy node (image_map). From there the repository's jobs run that entry's
image, so the mapping is a project setting and not a per-repository one — a
rerun of the skill that proposed it changes one line here rather than one
file in every repository.

The repository is one the project's local config lists (fugaro update --repo
onboards one), as owner/name or as a path inside its checkout, and the entry
is one this machine's catalog names (fugaro image add writes one). Setting a
repository that is already mapped replaces its entry; the file's map is the
project's whole map, so a map published from another machine is replaced by
this file's rather than added to.

This write is a person's own: fugaro update publishes it, and a coding
agent's session is refused it, in a managed project by that project's gate.

Usage: `fugaro image map set <repo> <entry>`

## `fugaro image promote`

Copy a repository's image definition into the catalog and point the repository at it

Read the repository's existing image definition, write it into the project's
image catalog as an entry, and point the repository's workflow at that entry
(image_name:), in the checkout you are in. Run it from the repository's own
checkout; the entry is named [name], else the repository's name.

Nothing is converted on its own: a repository's image: block or dockerfile:
keeps working untouched until this command is run for it, and fugaro update
never runs it. A definition taken from the workflow's image: block is
rendered and held in the entry (source: inline); a dockerfile: path stays a
pointer at that file (source: dockerfile), so the entry follows it.

The change to fugaro.yaml is a file in your working tree, not a commit: it is
yours to review and commit beside whatever else the same change carries.

This promote is not the promote step of a Cloud Build (images/derived/
cloudbuild.yaml): that step moves a build's latest tag onto the image it
just built, and this command copies a definition into the catalog. The two
share the word and nothing else.

Usage: `fugaro image promote <repo> [name]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for promote |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

## `fugaro image refresh`

Move a repository onto this release's base image: pin it, point the daily image check job at it, rebuild what is stale

Run it in the checkout of an onboarded repository, in your own terminal window
(or with --yes, unattended: see below).

It prints the whole plan first, then, each step with its own confirmation:
(2) resolves this release's base image of each selected workflow's kind at
its -pinned tag, verifies its cosign signature, reads the digest back
through the installation's remote repository and pins base_images.<kind> to
it, as fugaro update --base does (nothing is copied);
(3) points the repository's daily image check job at it (its image and
FUGARO_CHECK_SPEC's base images) through the Cloud Run Admin API, with no
Terraform; (4) rebuilds each selected workflow whose build record says it
was built from another base, or that has no build record or one that
cannot be read, each billable and asking no confirmation: it leases its
estimated cost from the project's budget before it is submitted, and a build
the cap has no room for is refused with the command that raises it — an
installation with no budget backend (budget.rtdb_url unset) has no lease to
take, and its builds are submitted uncounted);
(5) names fugaro update --anchor when fugaro.yaml lacks gcp_project.

A base_images entry that is neither this release's pin nor a release image
an earlier fugaro copied (a development or hand-pushed image) stops it
before anything changes, with or
without --yes: remove the entry from the local config, then rerun. It never
writes fugaro.yaml, never onboards a repository and never runs Terraform. A
coding agent's session is refused, --yes included (there is still no --json
or --plan-only to get around that). A run that stops says which steps
finished and what to rerun, --yes included when it was given; a rerun skips
what is done. Exit codes: 0 done, 1 a refusal or a confirmation not given,
2 a cloud failure.

Unattended use: pass --yes to run it from CI or a script, with no terminal.
It confirms every step that asks — the base pin and the check-job update;
the billable builds ask nothing in any session, and it is the budget lease
each of them takes that bounds them, where the installation has a budget
backend at all (with none, no build leases anything and none is counted).
Read the printed plan's build count first. --yes does not cover a coding
agent's session (refused,
same as without it) or a custom, dev or hand-pushed base image (still
refused with the one-line fix); there is still no --json or --plan-only.

Usage: `fugaro image refresh`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--ask` | bool | `false` | no | in a project whose marks say it is managed, ask the confirmations this run would otherwise skip (the project's name typed at each step that asks) instead of applying on the gate's verdict: a managed project asks nothing by default, and this is the flag that puts the questions back. It cannot restore a confirmation the billable builds no longer have: those ask nothing in any session, and each leases its cost from the project's budget where the installation has one. Refused where nobody can answer them (a coding agent's session, a pipe); a no-op with a sentence in a project that is not managed; refused beside --yes |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--expect-digest` | stringArray | `[]` | no | cross-check the digest of a base image's release signature, KIND=sha256:<hex>, as for the converge (repeatable) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for refresh |
| `--image-source` | string | "" | no | the registry and owner the release base images come from, as for the converge (default ghcr.io/dimipaun) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | owner/name (or a path inside its checkout) of the repository; it must be this checkout's origin (refresh reads fugaro.yaml from the checkout) |
| `--workflow` | stringArray | `[]` | no | a workflow to refresh (repeatable; default: every workflow in fugaro.yaml) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm every step that asks without asking (the base copy and the check-job update), and without a terminal: for CI or a script. The billable builds need no flag: they ask nothing in any session and each leases its cost from the project's budget where the installation has one. The plan is still printed first. Never confirmed in a coding agent's session (CLAUDECODE and the like): nothing is applied there, --yes included. Without --yes the steps that ask still need a real terminal, as always |

## `fugaro image rm`

Remove an image catalog entry from this machine's project config

Remove a named image from the project's image catalog, in this machine's
project config. The removal is refused while a repository's job still runs
the entry — because a workflow names it (image_name:), because the
project's image_map gives it to the repository, or because the tag-cover
rule picks it for the tags the workflow needs — since that job would then
be on an image no catalog describes. Point the repository at another entry
first (image_name: in its fugaro.yaml, or fugaro image map set), run
fugaro update, and remove the entry after.

Nothing is deleted from the registry: the entry's built image stays where
it is, and the next fugaro update publishes the catalog without the entry.

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |

## `fugaro image status`

Show each workflow's image: when it was built and from what, and its last daily check

For each workflow of the local config's repositories (or --repo's), print what
the runs bucket records: the image's build time and age, source commit and base

## `fugaro issue`

Read the issues saved on this machine, the ones you reported, and file one on GitHub

Read the issues saved on this machine.

An issue is one Markdown file under the user's state directory, holding
the whole issue: a strict header and the diagnosis' own words. `list`
shows what is saved, `show` prints one, `dismiss` sets one aside so
nothing is filed for it, `sync` uploads the ones this machine has not
uploaded yet, and `mine` reads the project's own store for the issues
this user reported. An issue is named by its local ID (`local-<run
stem>`) until it has been uploaded, and by its number (`#0007`) from
then on; `show`, `dismiss` and `submit` take either.

`submit` shows exactly what would be filed on GitHub — the post and the
sha256 of its bytes — and files nothing until `--ask` is answered with a
yes at your own terminal; without `gh`, it prints how to install it and
a new-issue link holding the same post instead.

An issue belongs to the project, not to one machine: once it has been
uploaded it is the project's store that says where it stands, so `list`
shows the whole team's issues and `show` prints the project's copy. To
get there, `sync` uploads this machine's own pending records to the
project's store, and `list`, `show` and `mine` — and `list --mine`,
which is the same read — do the same on the way to answering; a run
that cannot reach the store answers from the files here and says why.
Nothing is uploaded in a coding agent's session, and `sync` and
`dismiss` are refused there. Either way the text of a record is printed
as data: it comes from log text this machine did not write.

Usage: `fugaro issue`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for issue |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro issue dismiss` -- Mark an issue as not worth filing
- `fugaro issue list` -- List the project's issues, and the ones this machine has not uploaded yet
- `fugaro issue mine` -- List the issues this user reported, from the project's store
- `fugaro issue show` -- Print one issue: its number (#0007) or its local ID
- `fugaro issue submit` -- Show what would be filed on GitHub, and file it with --ask
- `fugaro issue sync` -- Upload the issues this machine saved and has not uploaded yet

## `fugaro issue dismiss`

Mark an issue as not worth filing

Mark one saved issue as not worth filing.

REF is the issue's number — `7`, or the `#0007` a listing prints — or
its local ID `local-<run stem>`, the same argument `show` takes. The
status is written in the issue's own file and nothing else changes: the
record stays where it is, so a listing still shows what was set aside
and who did it, and nothing is filed.

An issue is the project's, so one that has already been uploaded is set
aside in the project's store as well (F13): a teammate's listing shows
it as dismissed, and the decision does not have to be made again on
every machine. A store that cannot be reached is a line on stderr and
the dismissal here stands; a store that answers and refuses — the issue
is filed, or a teammate has decided it — refuses the command.

A number also names a teammate's issue, which this machine has no file
of: the rows `list` prints are the whole team's, so a reference that is
a number and no file here is read from the project's store and set
aside there (F23). A store that cannot be reached is then the refusal
rather than a line, there being nothing here to set aside instead.

An issue that has already been filed is refused: it is open on GitHub,
and setting it aside here would not close it.

A coding agent's session may not dismiss an issue: a steered diagnosis
could otherwise bury a real bug, so a person sets one aside (D1730).

Usage: `fugaro issue dismiss REF`

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for dismiss |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro issue list`

List the project's issues, and the ones this machine has not uploaded yet

List the issues the project holds, one row each.

An issue is the project's, not one machine's (spec 4b), so the rows are
the whole team's: the ones this machine saved and has not uploaded yet,
named by their local ID, and every issue of the project's store, named
by its number. A row names the issue the way `show`, `dismiss` and
`submit` take it, with the class the diagnosis gave it, where it stands,
and its one-line summary. Where the project's copy and this machine's
file disagree, the project's is printed: the store is the truth once an
issue is uploaded (F13), and a number is what `show` and `dismiss` read
from the store when this machine has no file of the issue.

A record this machine's folder holds for another project is not a row:
the folder is one for the whole machine, and another project's issue is
not this project's, nor is its number this listing's to print (F8b).

Listing uploads this machine's own pending issues first, exactly as
`mine` does: the same failure reported twice is one issue, and the one
still waiting here has to reach the store before it can be shown beside
the team's. A run that cannot reach the store lists this machine's own
records alone and says why on stderr, which leaves the table itself
clean for a reader and a script.

--mine lists the issues this user reported to the project instead: the
same rows `fugaro issue mine` prints, from the same read, so the two
commands answer with one listing (F12). --all goes with --mine and only
with it: this machine's own folder keeps every record until it is
deleted, and the 30-day rule is about the project's issues, not about
the files here.

Nothing is uploaded in a coding agent's session: the rows are this
machine's own records and the project is not read (F10, D1734).

--json prints the records themselves, in the shape
schemas/issue-record.schema.json describes — or, with --mine, the
document schemas/issue-mine.schema.json describes.

Usage: `fugaro issue list`

## `fugaro issue mine`

List the issues this user reported, from the project's store

List the issues this machine's user reported to the project.

The rows are the issues this user created and the ones their report was
merged into, read from the shared store the project's runs bucket keeps:
the number and the summary, where the issue stands, when it was hit,
submitted, resolved or dismissed, the link to the GitHub issue once it
has one, the release that fixed it and whether this machine is on it.
Other people who hit the issue are counted, never named.

A resolved issue this machine has not been updated to prints the one
command that fixes that — `fugaro update`. For one this machine already
has, the row offers the command this machine's own issue file recorded,
and nothing is run: the row is a listing.

An issue finished more than 30 days ago is hidden; --all shows it. With
the shared store unreadable — no network, no project selected — the rows
are the last successful read this machine cached, or the local files
alone, and the listing says which. In a coding agent's session only those
two are read and nothing is uploaded.

--json prints one versioned document, whose shape
schemas/issue-mine.schema.json describes. GitHub is read for nothing here:
the release a record names is what says an issue is fixed.

## `fugaro issue submit`

Show what would be filed on GitHub, and file it with --ask

Show exactly what would be filed on GitHub for one issue, or for every
issue that is still waiting.

REF is the issue's number — `7`, or the `#0007` a listing prints — or
its local ID `local-<run stem>`, the same argument `show` takes. With
no reference every `pending` issue is visited, and the ones already
filed or set aside are skipped.

The post is built once and printed as it is: the title, the body, and
the sha256 of the exact bytes. A run without --ask files nothing and
uploads nothing. --ask asks at your own terminal after showing the
preview and files exactly those bytes; a coding agent's session and a
pipe never file, because a confirmation nobody can answer is a refusal
and never a silent proceed.

--ask uploads this machine's own pending issues first, exactly as
`issue sync` does, and files the project's own record of a numbered
issue: the store is the truth once an issue is uploaded. The filing is
made under a claim on that record, so two people filing one issue at
the same moment file it once; a claim another submitter holds is
refused with who holds it and until when, and a record that changed
after the preview was shown is refused rather than filed unseen.

Filing needs GitHub's own `gh` with an account on github.com. Where it
is missing, or has no account there, the install command or `gh auth
login` is printed with the new-issue link holding the same title and
body; nothing is filed and the command exits non-zero.

Usage: `fugaro issue submit [REF]`

## `fugaro issue sync`

Upload the issues this machine saved and has not uploaded yet

Upload this machine's own pending issues to the project's store.

An issue is saved on the machine that hit the failure and uploaded
afterwards, so a run that was offline or that died before the upload
leaves it here. This is the command that retries those: each one takes
the project's next number, is renamed to it, and — when a teammate
already reported the same failure — is attached to their issue as one
more occurrence instead of becoming a second one.

An issue that cannot be uploaded stays where it is and is named in one
line, and the next run retries it: nothing here deletes an issue or
files one on GitHub.

A coding agent's session may not run this: uploading is a write to the
project's store, and a person runs `fugaro issue sync` (F10).

Act on a managed project: one Fugaro created with the coding agent's
confirmation refusal removed, where what may be applied is decided by a
deterministic gate over the saved plan rather than by a prompt.

This is not fugaro project (the project's own configuration) and not fugaro
setup (which creates and re-installs an installation): a managed project's
agent-authored root is applied by fugaro managed apply.

Usage: `fugaro managed`

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for managed |

- `fugaro managed apply` -- Apply the agent-authored Terraform root of a managed project, as the deployer account
- `fugaro managed flag` -- Flag an existing GCP project as managed (the project's owner)
- `fugaro managed status` -- Print a managed project's marks and its newest audit record

## `fugaro managed apply`

Apply the agent-authored Terraform root of a managed project, as the deployer account

Apply the agent-authored Terraform root ROOT of a managed project.

ROOT is a directory in this repository's checkout (the checkout whose
fugaro.yaml names the project). Its files are copied into this command's own
workdir — never run in place, so terraform's plan file, lock file and provider
directory are not written beside the configuration under review — the state
backend is set to the project's own managed state bucket, the root is planned
into a saved plan file, the plan is gated against the project's managed
allowlist and against the addresses the project's OWNER approved, and the saved
plan file is applied as the project's deployer service account.

An address this command may delete or replace is never one of this command's
arguments: an approval lives in the owner's object at
gs://<runs bucket>/fugaro/allow-delete.json, written with the operator's own
credentials by fugaro allow-delete. This command registers no flag for one, so
there is no way to pass one.

The refusal this command's apply does not carry is the coding agent's: in a
managed project a coding agent's session applies cloud changes with no human
prompt, and what replaces the prompt is the gate (a refused plan is not
applied), the marker (an unreadable one is not an apply), the owner's list (an
address the owner did not approve is refused) and the deployer account (which
holds no project-level IAM permission and cannot write the runs bucket). None
of the four is a boundary against a session that goes around this program.

The prompt comes back whenever the whole-project inventory does not clear the
project: before anything is planned, this command reads every resource of the
GCP project (Cloud Asset, with the operator's own credential) and compares it
with what the installation's Terraform states account for. A resource nothing
accounts for, or an inventory that cannot be read, keeps this run's
confirmation: a coding agent's session is refused and a person is asked, with
the reason printed first. Nothing is halted and nothing is deleted.

Usage: `fugaro managed apply ROOT`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for apply |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
