This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro managed flag`

Flag an existing GCP project as managed (the project's owner)

Flag an existing GCP project PROJECT_ID as managed, recording the managed
marker in that project's own runs bucket.

This is how a project Fugaro did not create becomes managed: the marker is
what tells a later run that this project's applies may skip the typed
confirmation, and it is normally written by the run that created the project
(fugaro setup --create-project --managed). Flagging is the after-the-fact way,
answered by the owner on 2026-10-16 (design D58).

Run it as an operator, with your own credentials. A coding agent's session is
refused, and so is a Fugaro run's process. The permission you give is the
PROJECT_ID argument itself: naming the exact GCP project ID on the command line
is the declaration that this project is managed (design D1541), and nothing is
typed at a prompt — this command registers no --yes and no --non-interactive,
so no flag stands in for naming the project either.

PROJECT_ID must be the exact GCP project ID of the installation selected by
--project, --config or the checkout: one invocation names one project, and
there is no bulk form, no wildcard and no prefix.

It records three things in gs://<runs bucket>/fugaro/managed.json: that this
project is managed, the monthly budget amount and currency the owner states
with --budget and --budget-currency, and the bound on the billable image
builds one invocation of fugaro image refresh may start (design D1013). The
amount is required, with no default (D64), because the marker's amount is what
the apply-time budget read opens the gate on: a marked project that records no
amount is refused by every managed apply rather than applied without a budget
control. The amount is the budget ALERT amount the installation's Terraform
creates and nothing else — this command does not create or change a budget,
and it makes no billing call. The bound is not a question: it is the marker's
own default of one build per invocation, and this command asks the owner for
no count, exactly as fugaro setup asks for none.

It writes BOTH marks a managed project carries, in one step: that object and
the label fugaro_managed=true on the GCP project itself (Task 3.0). The read
requires both — the label is what a project can be narrowed by, and a project
without it is not managed whatever its runs bucket holds — so writing the
object alone would leave this project exactly as unmanaged as it was. The
label is written on the project, by the account running this command, which is
why the account needs resourcemanager.projects.update on it; the project's
other labels are kept. A project that already carries that key with another
value is refused rather than overwritten — the label someone else put there is
a statement, not an empty slot — and the object written first is not taken
back, so that refusal says which half is there and which is missing.

What flagging gives up, stated before it writes: the marker is what turns the
typed confirmation off (D55), so from this project's next apply on, the
deterministic gate, the whole-project inventory, the owner-written delete list
(fugaro allow-delete) and the recorded budget are what stand in the
confirmation's place — and a coding agent's session can apply a plan the gate
admitted with no human prompt.

What it does not do: it is not a boundary against a session that goes around
this program. A coding agent's session holds the operator's credentials, can
write this object directly with gcloud storage cp, and can unset its own
marker and run this command; SECURITY.md records the wider Owner/Editor
bypass. The refusal below is a speed bump against an agent that uses the
program, not a wall against one that goes around it.

A project that already records an amount is refused: the amount is the owner's
decision at the time it was taken, and this command adds a budget rather than
editing one. The one object it does replace is a version-1 creation fact —
what fugaro setup --create-project without --managed leaves, and the state the
managed apply refuses for having no amount recorded. What it replaced is said
in the output, and the write is conditioned on the object it read, so nothing
is overwritten blind.

Usage: `fugaro managed flag PROJECT_ID`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--budget` | int64 | `0` | no | the monthly budget alert amount to record, in whole units of --budget-currency (required) |
| `--budget-currency` | string | "" | no | the currency --budget is in, three uppercase letters such as USD (required) |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for flag |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro managed status`

Print a managed project's marks and its newest audit record

Print whether the selected project is managed, and what its audit trail
records.

This is the read a screen of a managed project is built on: one closed document
about one project, holding the two marks' own answer and the bounded subset of
the newest audit record — never a sentence to be parsed, whose next rewording
would change what a screen draws.

The document also carries this machine's record of the project's last plain
"fugaro update": what that update retired by itself, when it settled the
retirement and how many runs the registry held while it did, with the record's
own version beside it — or a sentence instead of the entry when that record
cannot be read, so a record that is corrupt is never drawn as a project nothing
was recorded for. It is a local read, and it is made whatever the marks answer:
a project that is not managed runs updates too.

It reads the same two facts a managed apply reads, and changes no cloud object:
whether the project is managed is the creation fact in its runs bucket and the
fugaro_managed label on the project itself, which have to agree, and the trail
is the records the managed commands file under gs://<runs bucket>/fugaro/managed-audit/.

The trail is the newest record of the current UTC day, and of the previous day
when today holds nothing, with the day and that day's count beside it. A day
whose records could not be read is said rather than shown as an empty one: the
two are different facts and only one of them is a reason to look further. A
project that is not managed files no record at all, so its trail is not read and
nothing is reported about it — and a project whose marker or label was removed
is "not managed", never "revoked", which is a run-time decision of the gate and
is recorded nowhere.

What it prints is bounded on purpose: the record's time, its command, the gate's
verdict, the account the write ran as and the plan digest. The record's argv is
never printed, by this command or by anything that reads this document: it holds
paths and titles an operator did not mean to publish.

--json prints the document, which the desktop console reads as bytes: see the
desktop console's JSON contract, section 6.21, for every member and what its
emptiness means.

Usage: `fugaro managed status`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for status |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro managed unflag`

Remove both marks that make a GCP project managed (the project's owner)

Remove the marks that make GCP project PROJECT_ID a managed project.

A managed project carries two marks, written together by the run that created
it (fugaro setup --create-project --managed) or by fugaro managed flag: the
creation fact gs://<runs bucket>/fugaro/managed.json in that project's own runs
bucket, and the label fugaro_managed=true on the GCP project itself. The read
requires both, so the project is managed only while the two are there — and
unflagging removes both, in one command, so an owner never has to do the
deletion and the label write by hand.

A project that is already half-removed — the state a manual removal leaves,
with the object gone and the label there, or the reverse — is converged rather
than refused: which half was already gone is said, and the other is removed.
After this command the project is not managed, and its applies take the typed
confirmation again.

What it does not remove is the deployer fence. The seven scoped roles and their
conditioned bindings stay in the project and in the installation, and fugaro
update --forget stays refused for a fenced installation. This command makes no
IAM call at all; undoing the fence is not revocation and is not offered here
(docs/design/managed-projects.md §10.2).

Run it in your own terminal, as an operator, with your own credentials. The
permission you give is the PROJECT_ID argument itself: it names the one project
whose marks come off, and nothing stands in for naming it — not --yes, not
--non-interactive, not a pipe. A coding agent's session is refused, and a
Fugaro run's own process is refused.

PROJECT_ID must be the exact GCP project ID of the installation selected by
--project, --config or the checkout: one invocation names one project, and
there is no bulk form, no wildcard and no prefix.

Usage: `fugaro managed unflag PROJECT_ID`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for unflag |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro models`

Show the models this project can run, and where each is served

Show the models this project can name and the routes behind them.

The routes are the owner's providers in the project config, each with the
models it claims, its fee and the repositories whose code may be sent to it,
beside the direct Anthropic route. The models are the ones a run can name
today: an ID a route claims, a model_prices key, a budget.allowed_models entry
and a model a repository pins.

Both reads are offline: they touch no bucket, no database and no host. What
they print about the cloud is what the local files already say.

Usage: `fugaro models`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for models |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro models add` -- Let this project run a model: claim it on a route and price it
- `fugaro models ls` -- Show this project's routes, its models and what each repository runs
- `fugaro models rm` -- Stop letting this project run a model: drop its claim, price and allow-list entry
- `fugaro models search` -- Find a model in the built-in price catalog and the Claude table
- `fugaro models use` -- Point one repository's own config at a model, in its working tree

## `fugaro models add`

Let this project run a model: claim it on a route and price it

Add a model to this project's own config.

The model ID is appended to a route's models — the exact ID, never a
pattern — and a model the built-in price catalog does not price needs
--price-in and --price-out (dollars per million tokens), which write a
model_prices entry. When budget.allowed_models is set the ID is appended to
it; when it is absent it stays absent.

Only the keys it changes are rewritten: every comment and every other key of
the file is kept.

The change reaches a run through `fugaro update`, which publishes the policy
node: a model_prices entry and a budget.allowed_models entry are what a run
reads from there. A route's own claim is not — a run routes by the copy of
the providers block in its job's environment — so a repository routes to the
model once `fugaro update --repo .` has been run in its checkout.

Usage: `fugaro models add <id>`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for add |
| `--price-in` | float64 | `0` | no | input price, dollars per million tokens (required for a model the catalog does not price) |
| `--price-out` | float64 | `0` | no | output price, dollars per million tokens (required for a model the catalog does not price) |
| `--route` | string | "" | no | the route that claims the model (default: the route that claims it already, or the only one) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the write without a prompt |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro models ls`

Show this project's routes, its models and what each repository runs

Show, offline, what this project can run.

ROUTES is the owner's providers in the project config — the host, the models
each claims, its route_fee_pct and the repositories whose code may be sent to
it — beside the direct Anthropic route. MODELS is every model a run can name
today (a route's claim, a model_prices key, a budget.allowed_models entry, a
repository's pin), with the route that serves it, where its price comes from
and what it costs. ALLOW-LISTS is which repositories each model may be sent
to. USAGE is each recorded repository's pins, read out of the fugaro.yaml at
the base branch it runs against.

A repository this machine has no checkout for is unknown, never guessed at.
The command reaches no bucket, no database and no host.

## `fugaro models rm`

Stop letting this project run a model: drop its claim, price and allow-list entry

Remove a model from this project's own config.

The model's exact entry is dropped from the route's models, its model_prices
entry and its budget.allowed_models entry. A pattern that claims the model
is left, and the command says so: the model stays usable until the route's
own list stops covering it.

A repository that pins the model is not refused (D783). It is a warning:
the repositories this machine can read that pin it are named, with the role
each names it in, and so are the repositories it cannot read. The next run
of each one fails at launch with no provider for the model, until the pin is
changed with `fugaro models use` or the model is added back.

Only the keys it changes are rewritten: every comment and every other key of
the file is kept. `fugaro update` publishes the policy node, which carries the
model_prices and budget.allowed_models halves of the removal to the runs that
read it; the route's own claims are in the copy of the providers block each
job holds, so a repository stops routing to the model when `fugaro update
--repo .` is run in its checkout.

Usage: `fugaro models rm <id>`

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for rm |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the write without a prompt |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro models use`

Point one repository's own config at a model, in its working tree

Prepare the change to a repository's own fugaro.yaml that makes one role run
a model, in the checkout's working tree for the owner to review and commit.

The switch is judged the way a launch judges it: a route of the project config
must claim the model and its allow_data_to must name the repository, the model
must be priced, budget.allowed_models must admit it, and the repository's own
agent.auth and budget must support a provider model. A failure is a refusal
with nothing written, and the message names the `fugaro models add` that would
fix a missing claim or price.

Only agent.models.<role> changes: every comment and every other byte of the
file is kept. The command never commits, pushes or opens a pull request — the
change reaches runs when the owner's own branch is merged to the base branch,
which is what every run reads.

Usage: `fugaro models use <repo> <coder|reviewer|background|vision> <id>`

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for use |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the write without a prompt |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro orchestrator`

Read and patch the project's orchestrator state

Read the project's orchestrator state, its audit log, and write the typed
patch a person or a session may write. The state is the document the
project's daemon keeps in its Firebase Realtime Database
(orchestrator/<project>/{state,lease,audit}), and this command acts as
the person the Application Default Credentials belong to, so the
database's own roles decide what it may read and write.

state prints the generated summary of the live node; --brief prints only
that summary, and --brief --offline prints the brief the daemon cached at
session start instead, reaching no network at all. events reads the audit
log. patch applies one document from -f, and the ops only a person may
land (approving a work item, setting the goal, closing a decision that
waits on a person) are confirmed at a real terminal with the project's
name typed, never by --yes: a session that has none writes nothing.
import loads the one-time session dump, validated as a patch and refused
the person's own ops: no dump approves work.

run is the daemon itself, in the foreground. install, uninstall and
status are the login unit that keeps it running: the three read no
project and reach no network, and they write no system path and need no
root — the unit is one file under your own home and the service manager
is asked at your own login level.

Usage: `fugaro orchestrator`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for orchestrator |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro orchestrator events` -- Read the orchestrator's audit log
- `fugaro orchestrator import` -- Load the one-time session dump into the orchestrator's state
- `fugaro orchestrator install` -- Install or re-render the login unit that runs the daemon
- `fugaro orchestrator ls` -- List the installation's orchestrators
- `fugaro orchestrator patch` -- Apply one typed patch document to the orchestrator's state
- `fugaro orchestrator run` -- Run the project's orchestrator daemon in the foreground
- `fugaro orchestrator state` -- Print the orchestrator's state: the generated summary of its live node
- `fugaro orchestrator status` -- Report the login unit that runs the daemon
- `fugaro orchestrator uninstall` -- Remove the login unit that runs the daemon

## `fugaro orchestrator import`

Load the one-time session dump into the orchestrator's state

Load the one-time session dump (the spec's Migration) into the project's
orchestrator state, from -f's file or from stdin with -f -. The dump is one
patch document (schemas/orchestrator-patch.schema.json) a session wrote out,
and it is read by the same validator and bounded by the same caps as
fugaro orchestrator patch: it is the one document in this loop written by a
model, and everything it carries is data, never an instruction.

The dump lands as the person who runs this, because the migration is theirs
to make, and it lands nothing a session may not land: approving a work
item, setting the goal and closing a decision that waits on anyone but a
session are the person's own word, given at a real terminal over the spec
they read (fugaro orchestrator patch). So no dump approves work and no dump
closes a decision of the person's — not even one the dump raises and closes
itself — and every work item the dump declares arrives unapproved.

Usage: `fugaro orchestrator import`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `-f`, `--file` | string | "" | no | the session dump to import, or - to read it from stdin |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for import |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro orchestrator install`

Install or re-render the login unit that runs the daemon

Write the per-user login unit that runs `fugaro orchestrator run` and load
it, so the daemon starts at every login and is restarted when it stops.
Nothing else is written: no system path is touched, no root is needed, and
the service manager is asked at your own login level (launchd on macOS,
systemd --user on Linux; Windows has neither, and answers so).

The unit names the stable path of this fugaro — Homebrew's opt link and
never a versioned Cellar path that an upgrade removes — twice: as the
program to run, and as the `--binary` argument whose version the daemon
compares with its own before it hands over to a new release.

It is idempotent: a unit that is already there is re-rendered from this
release's template and the service restarted, which is also what `fugaro
update` does to an installed unit (and `fugaro update` never installs
one). It writes no state and migrates none: the daemon's own start-up
does that.

A unit is code that runs at every login, so this command asks you to type
the word install at a real terminal, has no flag that stands in for it,
and refuses in a coding agent's session. Running it yourself, without the
marker, is the way to do it: whoever can do that can write the file by
hand anyway.

Usage: `fugaro orchestrator install`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for install |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro orchestrator ls`

List the installation's orchestrators

List the orchestrators this installation has: every id whose node exists in
the project's database, with the holder of its lease and when that holder last
beat, and every cached brief this machine holds, with the time the daemon wrote
it. An orchestrator this machine runs — one with a cached brief — is `local`;
one only the database holds is `central`. A cached brief of an id nothing is
beating any more is marked stale: the daemon that wrote it has stopped driving
the id, so no cycle is rewriting it. --json prints a versioned document
(schemas/orchestrator-output.schema.json).

There is no registry of processes and no port: the node and the cache file are
the two things the daemon writes, and a run or a token may not read either.

Usage: `fugaro orchestrator ls`

## `fugaro orchestrator patch`

Apply one typed patch document to the orchestrator's state

Apply one patch document (schemas/orchestrator-patch.schema.json) to the
project's orchestrator state, from -f's file or from stdin with -f -. The
document is validated and applied by the state model's own code, and the write
is conditional on the revision this run read, so a patch built from a state
somebody else has since changed is refused rather than landed on top of it.

A run acts as a session. The ops only a person may land — approving a work
item, setting the goal, and closing a decision that waits on a person — are
confirmed at a real terminal, where the project's name is typed over the write
that lands: the spec an approval binds, and every op the document carries,
because the whole of it lands as the person who confirms it. Every other
session, --json, a pipe and a coding agent's environment are refused and write
nothing, and --yes never covers them.
No flag, environment variable or field of the document makes this command the
daemon or the decision agent: the daemon's bookkeeping is the daemon's.

Usage: `fugaro orchestrator patch`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `-f`, `--file` | string | "" | no | the patch document to apply, or - to read it from stdin |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for patch |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

## `fugaro orchestrator run`

Run the project's orchestrator daemon in the foreground

Run the project's orchestrator daemon: take the id's lease, tick every
interval — and sooner when the database's own stream says the node moved —
start the runs the state's plan calls for over the same launch path fugaro
run takes, and rewrite the session-start cache after every cycle. It stops
when the lease goes to another machine, and it exits cleanly (releasing the
lease) when the binary the unit names has moved on, so the login unit starts
the new one.

The command is the person's own credential and the daemon's own loop: it
never converges, publishes or installs anything, and a state node this
release does not read is reported as an update being due rather than
touched. Run it in the foreground to watch it; the login unit is what keeps
it running (fugaro setup installs it).

Usage: `fugaro orchestrator run`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--binary` | string | "" | no | the stable path of the fugaro binary the login unit names: the daemon exits cleanly when the version there differs from this process |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for run |
| `--interval` | duration | `30s` | no | how long to wait between cycles when the node says nothing moved |
| `--once` | bool | `false` | no | run one cycle and exit, releasing the lease, instead of driving the id until it is stopped |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro orchestrator uninstall`

Remove the login unit that runs the daemon

Unload the login unit and delete its file, so the daemon stops being
started at login and stops being restarted. It asks nothing: removing the
unit takes away code that runs at every login rather than adding it, and
`fugaro orchestrator install` writes it back after its own typed
confirmation.

Nothing else is touched: the project's orchestrator state, its lease and
its audit log are in the database and not in the unit, `fugaro orchestrator
run` still runs in the foreground without a unit, and a machine with no
unit installed is not an error — it says so and returns.

## `fugaro pair`

Pair a phone with this installation

Pair a phone with this installation: the operator shows a QR code, the
phone scans it, writes its public key and shows a code derived from that
key, and the operator types the code back to bind the two.

Pairing is an admin act, and it needs both of the installation's two role
sets: the signer account's fugaroTokenMinter role to mint the pairing
token and the device token, and roles/firebasedatabase.admin to write the
device node and the delivery node.

Pairing is discovery, not identity: scanning the code tells the phone which
project and database to connect to and grants it no access by itself.

The code carries no key. The final credentials — the device token, the
per-pairing MAC key and the configuration the app stores — go to the phone
encrypted to the key it generated, and the MAC key never leaves this
laptop's OS keychain in clear, is never printed, and is not in the code.

The typed code is the binding: nothing is written to the project before the
code the operator types matches the key the phone wrote, so a refused
pairing leaves the project exactly as it was.

The code is drawn in a terminal wide enough for it. The payload is over a
kilobyte, so its code is over a hundred columns wide, and a narrower
terminal gets the payload line instead of a drawing that would wrap and
stop being a QR code; --json carries that same payload for a console.

Its own state is the local config: the project, its database URL and
Identity Toolkit API key, and the signer account. --json streams the
pairing as one JSON object per line on stdout for a console to read;
the console has asked the operator for the code itself, and the command
takes the code back as one line on stdin.

Usage: `fugaro pair`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |

## `fugaro pair ls`

List the devices paired with this installation

List the devices paired with this installation: one row per device node
under config/admin/devices, with the uid (a key, and therefore printable),
the name, the administered email, the role and the pairing time.

It reads with roles/firebasedatabase.admin, and it prints no token, no key
and no keychain item's value: the node holds none of them, and the item's
name is not in the node either, so there is nothing else to print.

It does not report whether a device's Auth user still exists. The Auth user
is not in the database, so database admin does not reach it, and the node's
existence is the whole of what the rules read (D166): an orphaned Auth user
whose node is gone is the history sweep's business and is invisible to the
rules by construction.

Its own state is the local config, as it is for the rest of the command.

Usage: `fugaro pair ls`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for ls |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print the pairings as one JSON event on stdout |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro pair revoke`

Revoke a paired device

Revoke a paired device: the phone is off this installation's allowlist from
its next request on.

The order is the command (M4): the device node under config/admin/devices
goes first, because the node's existence is what the rules read and its
deletion revokes at once, without waiting for an ID token to expire; then
this laptop's OS keychain item for that pairing's MAC key. Two deletions,
and both are here.

The pairing session's own node is not one of them. Its key is the p~ uid
the session drew, and nothing on this laptop records that uid, so a revoke
by device cannot name the node it would delete; the history sweep deletes
it with the p~ user the node belongs to (mobile plan decision 2), and it
is the sweep this command names rather than a node it did not touch.

It does not delete the device's Auth user. No role a Terraform grant gives
an operator can delete one (the history job's account is the only holder of
roles/firebaseauth.admin), and the device node's deletion is what makes the
orphan the history sweep's to remove — which is why this command names the
sweep rather than pretending the account is gone.

Exactly one of --uid and --name selects the device, and a --name that
matches more than one node is refused rather than revoked ambiguously: the
refusal says how many it matched, and `fugaro pair ls` prints the uids to
pick one from.

Its own state is the local config, as it is for the rest of the command.

Usage: `fugaro pair revoke (--uid UID | --name NAME)`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for revoke |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print the revocation as one JSON event on stdout |
| `--name` | string | "" | no | the name of the device to revoke; it must match exactly one device |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--uid` | string | "" | no | the uid of the device to revoke (m~…), which is the node's key |

## `fugaro plan graph`

Print a plan's graph: its tasks, their dependencies and their footprints

Print the graph artifact written beside a plan.

The artifact is `<plan>.graph.json` — for docs/plans/foo.md it is
docs/plans/foo.graph.json. With no --plan, the one graph artifact under
docs/plans/ is read; more than one is refused rather than guessed at.

A graph this build does not understand is refused rather than rendered: a
future schema version, a malformed document, an edge to a node that is not
there, or a cycle.

When the plan ran the contract-first decoupling pass, the read prints that
pass's own record too: every edge the pass broke with the contract and the
integration task that cover it, what the break bought measured before and
after, and the contract stubs still in the checkout. A plan that broke no
edge prints none of it.

The read also answers what the planner cannot: each task's level, whether it
is ready or blocked, and the plan's critical path. A task is ready when every
task it needs is done, so --done names the tasks that are — an id the graph
does not carry is refused rather than ignored. This is a local read and it
writes nothing.

Usage: `fugaro plan graph`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--done` | stringSlice | `[]` | no | the tasks whose work is done, by id (comma-separated or repeated); a task is ready when every task it needs is done |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for graph |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--plan` | string | "" | no | the plan document the graph sits beside (default: the one graph artifact under docs/plans) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro plan status`

Print every plan's tasks, joined to the runs working on them

Print every plan's graph under docs/, with each task's state from the runs.

A task's state joins the graph to the runs bucket of the selected project:
running with the stage of the run working on it, done when the run's pull
request is merged, cancelled when the task's only run was, blocked while a
task it needs is not done, ready when the work can start (the task a launch
may act on), and not-started otherwise.

A run joins a task by the --plan-task its launch recorded, and only when it
is a run of this checkout's own repository: a run of another repository
naming the same task is ignored. The join is display-only — nothing here
makes another plan's task ready.

Every run the bucket still holds (ninety days) is listed. Only the runs that
join a task of a plan here have their pull requests looked up, so the
lookups cost what the plans hold rather than what the repository's history
holds, and one read asks about at most 32 pull requests, the newest runs'
first.

Whether a pull request is merged is asked of your own gh, when it is
installed, and only about a pull request of this checkout's own
repository: a run that recorded another repository's pull request is not
merged here. Where gh cannot answer (a Bitbucket repository, no gh, a
lookup that failed, one past the 32) a task whose run recorded a ready pull
request shows done with the mark "merge unknown" rather than nothing.

Two artifacts that would be one plan id — docs/plans/foo.graph.json and
docs/plans/foo/bar.graph.json both give plans/foo — cannot be joined apart,
so the second is not listed and a warning names both.

Merged and cancelled tasks are counted per release and not listed; --all
lists them too. This command writes nothing.

Usage: `fugaro plan status`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--all` | bool | `false` | no | list the closed tasks too (merged and cancelled) instead of counting them per release |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for status |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

## `fugaro project clone-url rm`

Take a repository's clone URL away

Remove one entry of the project's clone_urls block, in this machine's
project config file. The other entries stand, and the change reaches a run
through `fugaro update`.

The last entry is not this command's to take away. An empty block is how a
project states that it gives no repository a URL, and the one spelling of
one — an empty mapping, `clone_urls: {}` — is not one this release's editor
writes; a key left with no entry under it is read as a file that says
nothing about the block, which keeps the published node's, so removing the
last entry would change nothing at all. That removal is therefore refused,
and the refusal names the one line that states it — put `clone_urls: {}` in
the file by hand, and run `fugaro update`.

Usage: `fugaro project clone-url rm <provider>/<owner>/<name>`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for rm |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the write without a prompt |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro project clone-url set`

Give a repository the URL its runs clone from

Write one entry of the project's clone_urls block, in this machine's
project config file.

The repository is named canonically — <provider>/<owner>/<name>, the spelling
the allow-list and the CLI use everywhere — and the URL must be an https URL
without credentials that names exactly that repository on that provider's own
host. A URL naming another repository, or another host, is refused before
anything is written: the URL is where a run clones from, while its slug, its
locks, its cache and its budget session all name the repository its own
task.json does, and a run that cloned from elsewhere while doing this
repository's work is the thing the node's own rule exists to refuse.

The change reaches a run through `fugaro update`, which publishes the policy
node the runner reads.

Usage: `fugaro project clone-url set <provider>/<owner>/<name> <url>`

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for set |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the write without a prompt |

## `fugaro project policy publish`

Publish the project's policy from the operator's config (budget admins)

Build the project's policy from this machine's project config — the budget
block, the providers (their secrets by NAME, never a value), the model_prices
overrides and the allow-list — and write it to config/policy/shared with an
ETag-guarded write. The diff follows the write: it is printed once the node
holds the policy, and a write that failed prints no diff — the node is as it
was, and the command says so. From then on the node is the
ceiling for every key it names, and a key it leaves out keeps the value the
job's environment was deployed with.

Publishing refuses without the rules marker (config/limits/policyRules): a
policy published before the rules are deployed is one the runs it bounds
cannot read, so run fugaro update with a Fugaro that deploys them first. It
also refuses a node written by a newer Fugaro.

allow_repos is seeded from this machine's repos: map and from the shared
config's repository list, and only when the node is absent or --seed-repos is
passed: a later publish never re-adds a name an operator removed. It is never
seeded from the bucket's runs/<slug>/ prefixes, which every run of a profile
can write.

--delete removes the policy (the children first, the shared node last, so a
launch mid-delete still sees the policy and keeps its tighter ceiling) and
puts the project back on the ceiling its jobs' environments carry. It goes
through the same rules-marker gate as a publish, refuses without --yes while
runs are in flight, and asks you to type the project's name otherwise. The
config/policy/repos children are removed too, shared node or not: a delete
that failed on the shared node leaves them behind, and this is what clears
them.

Each repository an account a profile names admits also gets a child under
config/policy/repos/$slug, holding the NAMES of its admitted accounts and
nothing else: the accounts published are the ones some profile names,
qualified by that profile's provider, so an account this config defines but
no profile names admits nothing a run could read. The children are narrowed before the shared node and widened
after it, so a publish that stops between the two writes leaves the installation tighter than the config asked, never looser.
When the node this publish writes carries a member an older Fugaro refuses
whole — a credentials
block, or routing.claude.via: cascade — the diff warns: older launchers (and,
for the cascade, older runner images) stop until they are upgraded.

routing.claude is written where the operator writes it: this config. A
publish refuses to drop an active route the config does not account for, and
refuses to turn the credentials cascade off — a node carrying
routing.claude.via: cascade with a config that names no Claude switch is
refused with its own sentence, because the cascade is not a route: it decides
which credential carries a Claude call, never where the call goes, and it is
what hands a run the project's other credentials. A config that writes a
routing block naming no Claude switch in the same state is refused too.
--remove-routing is how the operator says the block goes away on purpose.

Usage: `fugaro project policy publish [--seed-repos] [--delete] [--yes] [--remove-routing]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--delete` | bool | `false` | no | remove the published policy (project-centric mode off again) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for publish |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--remove-routing` | bool | `false` | no | drop the published policy's routing block on purpose (an active route stops being taken) |
| `--seed-repos` | bool | `false` | no | seed allow_repos from the operator's repositories again |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the deletion without typing the project's name |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro project profile add`

Define a job profile: the shape a workflow's job is deployed as

Define a job profile in this project's own config.

The four values are the job's whole shape and all four are required: one
Cloud Run job per (profile, provider, account) is deployed with them, and a
profile missing one of them describes no job at all. The provider is one of
the git providers Fugaro has a path for, because it is part of the job's
identity, of the slug its runs are stored under and of the credential the job
holds.

The profile is checked against the same rules the publisher applies to the
published policy, so what it writes is what `fugaro update` will deploy: the
name, the provider, the Cloud Run shape of cpu and memory, and the timeout
within Cloud Run's ceiling. A config that carries a profiles: block must
define standard, which is the profile every workflow that names none runs on.

The block reaches a run through the published policy, so the change is
deployed by `fugaro update`, which publishes it and deploys the jobs.

Only the keys it writes are rewritten: every comment and every other key of
the file is kept.

Usage: `fugaro project profile add NAME --provider P --cpu N --memory M --timeout-class C`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--cpu` | int | `0` | no | the vCPUs the job's Cloud Run task gets |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for add |
| `--memory` | string | "" | no | the memory the job's task gets, for example 4Gi |
| `--provider` | string | "" | no | the git provider the profile's job serves (github, gitlab, bitbucket or fake) |
| `--timeout-class` | string | "" | no | the job's task timeout, for example 6h |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the write without a prompt |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

List the job profiles this project's own config defines.

Each line is one profile: the provider and the Cloud Run shape its job is
deployed as, the secrets the job mounts (by NAME — a config carries no value),
the repositories it admits, and the Claude accounts it serves. The line after
it says which jobs it maps to: one per (profile, provider, account).

A config with no profiles: block defines none, and a policy built from it
sets no profile at all — every workflow then runs on the job its own
environment names.

The read is offline: it opens this machine's project config and nothing else.

Usage: `fugaro project profile ls [--json]`

## `fugaro project profile rm`

Remove a job profile no workflow selects

Remove a job profile from this project's own config.

The removal is refused while a workflow this machine can read selects the
profile: a workflow whose job_profile the published policy does not define
has every run refused at start, one run at a time, at the launcher rather
than here. Change the workflow's job_profile first, then remove the profile.

A repository this machine holds no checkout for cannot be read, so it is
named as unread rather than assumed: a workflow of one may still select the
profile, and its next run says so.

Removing the last profile takes the profiles: block with it, which is how a
config says it sets no profile at all. Only the keys it removes are
rewritten: every comment and every other key of the file is kept.

Usage: `fugaro project profile rm NAME`

## `fugaro project profile set`

Change one key of one job profile

Change one key of one job profile in this project's own config.

KEY is one of the profile's own keys — provider, cpu, memory, timeout_class,
secrets, allow_repos, claude_accounts — and VALUE is what it becomes. The
three list keys take a comma-separated list, and an empty VALUE removes the
key rather than writing a list with nothing in it: absent secrets mount
nothing, and an absent allow_repos falls back to the project's own list,
where a written empty one is ambiguous and refused.

Every other key and every comment of the file is kept. The edited block is
held to the rules the publisher applies to the published policy, so a profile
this writes is one `fugaro update` publishes. The deployer then holds the
jobs it builds to rules of its own beyond those — a secret a job mounts has
to be one stored project-wide, which project_secrets decides — so a profile
that publishes is not always one whose job deploys.

Usage: `fugaro project profile set NAME KEY VALUE`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for set |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the write without a prompt |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro project repos add`

Enroll a repository: add it to the policy's allow-list

Add a canonical repository (github/acme/app, bitbucket/acme/*) to the
published policy's allow_repos, through the same ETag-guarded write the
publisher uses, and print the change. A bare owner/name takes its provider
from this machine's project config, and * is the list's own entry for every
repository: it is written as it is. Only allow_repos changes.

Usage: `fugaro project repos add <provider/owner/name | owner/name | *>`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for add |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro project repos rm`

Un-enroll a repository: remove it from the allow-list

Remove an entry from the published policy's allow_repos. Removing an allowed
repository stops its runs — a run of a repository the list does not admit is
refused before it mints a git token — unless another entry on the list still
admits it, which is the case a pattern makes (github/acme/app stays admitted
while github/acme/* is there); the confirmation says which of the two it is.
Removing * refuses every repository the rest of the list does not admit.
So it asks you to type the project's name, and while a run is in flight --yes
alone is not enough.

Usage: `fugaro project repos rm <provider/owner/name | owner/name | *>`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for rm |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the removal without typing the project's name (not while a run is in flight) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro project repos set`

Write a repository's workflow selection or a job profile, in this machine's project config

Write one of the two shapes the generic writer cannot express, in this
machine's project config:

    fugaro project repos set acme/app --workflows web,docs
    fugaro project repos set --job-profile gpu --provider github --cpu 4 \
        --memory 8Gi --timeout-class 12h --secrets acme-db --allow-repos acme/app

A repository's workflows selection says which of the repository's own workflows
this project runs, and it is written WHOLE: the names given are the selection,
so a second run replaces it rather than adding to it. The repository is one the
project's config lists (fugaro update --repo onboards one); a name it does not
list is refused, because a selection stored under a name nothing looks up is a
line nobody sees fail.

A job profile is what a Cloud Run job is deployed as, addressed by name
(D1163): the seven keys are provider, cpu, memory, timeout_class, secrets,
allow_repos and claude_accounts, and the flags below write them. The block is
created when the config does not hold one under that name, and a NEW profile
must name its own --provider: a profile with no provider is one no job of it can
be deployed, and fugaro project policy publish refuses such a policy.

What a profile's values owe — a known provider, a cpu/memory shape Cloud Run
serves, a duration timeout_class — is the policy's own rule
(projectpolicy.validProfiles), applied by fugaro project policy publish and read
back by every run; this command writes the file and refuses only what the file
itself would not read.

The repos.* scalars and lists are the generic writer's (D1173):

    fugaro settings set repos.acme/app.base_branch main
    fugaro settings set repos.acme/app.workflows --add docs

This write is a person's own: fugaro update publishes it, and a coding agent's
session is refused it, in a managed project by that project's gate.

Every write ends with one line: next: fugaro update.

Usage: `fugaro project repos set (REPO --workflows NAME[,NAME...]) | (--job-profile NAME [members])`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--allow-repos` | stringSlice | `[]` | no | profiles.NAME.allow_repos: the repositories the profile serves, comma-separated; the list is written whole |
| `--ask` | bool | `false` | no | in a project whose marks say it is managed, ask the confirmation this write would otherwise get instead of writing on the gate's verdict: a managed project asks nothing by default, and this is the flag that puts the question back. Refused where nobody can answer it (a coding agent's session, a pipe, --non-interactive); a no-op with a sentence in a project that is not managed; refused beside --yes |
| `--claude-accounts` | stringSlice | `[]` | no | profiles.NAME.claude_accounts: the Claude accounts the profile serves, comma-separated; the list is written whole |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--cpu` | int | `0` | no | profiles.NAME.cpu: the Cloud Run cpu count the job is deployed with |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for set |
| `--job-profile` | string | "" | no | the job profile to write, by name; with it, the members below write the block's keys |
| `--memory` | string | "" | no | profiles.NAME.memory: the Cloud Run memory the job is deployed with, e.g. 4Gi |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--provider` | string | "" | no | profiles.NAME.provider: the git provider the profile's job holds a credential for (required for a new profile) |
| `--secrets` | stringSlice | `[]` | no | profiles.NAME.secrets: the Secret Manager names the profile's job mounts, comma-separated; the list is written whole |
| `--timeout-class` | string | "" | no | profiles.NAME.timeout_class: the job's task timeout as a duration, e.g. 6h or 90m |
| `--workflows` | stringSlice | `[]` | no | repos.REPO.workflows: which of the repository's own workflows this project runs, comma-separated; the selection is written whole |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the write without a prompt |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro project routing`

The project's Claude routing switch: where a run's Claude calls go

Usage: `fugaro project routing`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for routing |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro project routing set` -- Set the route this project's Claude calls take
- `fugaro project routing show` -- Show the route this project's Claude calls take
- `fugaro project routing unset` -- Remove the routing switch, when it carries nothing

## `fugaro project routing set`

Set the route this project's Claude calls take

Set the Claude routing switch in this project's own config.

--models names the Claude IDs the switch carries, comma-separated; a route
(openrouter, auto) needs an explicit list, because the list is the opt-in and
an empty one would opt every Claude model in (D1a/D1b). cascade takes no list
at all — it decides which credential carries a call, never where the call goes
(O3) — and direct reads one as inert, so both drop it: a route that goes away
with it is what setting the switch is.

via: cascade keeps every call going to Anthropic and hands the credential
choice to the credentials service: an exhausted shared subscription token is
replaced by the next usable credential, and with credentials.fallback: auto
that reaches the paid tiers.

Sending the switch to a route is a data-egress change and is the widening of
this block: a coding agent's session writes it to no document, whatever --yes
says, and a narrowing (direct, cascade, an unset) is the owner's ordinary
write.

The change reaches a run through `fugaro update`, which publishes the policy
node every run reads its route from. Only the keys it writes are rewritten:
every comment and every other key of the file is kept.

Usage: `fugaro project routing set claude --via direct|cascade|openrouter|auto [--models ...]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for set |
| `--models` | string | "" | no | the Claude IDs a route carries, comma-separated (required for openrouter and auto) |
| `--via` | string | "" | no | the route: direct, cascade, openrouter or auto |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the write without a prompt |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro project routing show`

Show the route this project's Claude calls take

Show the Claude routing switch this project's own config carries.

via: cascade keeps every call going to Anthropic under the ID a pin names and
lets the credentials service decide which credential carries it; via:
openrouter and via: auto send the Claude IDs the switch lists to the provider
entry that claims them, and only that entry's allow_data_to decides which
repositories' code may be sent there; via: direct, and no switch at all, route
nothing and every call goes to Anthropic.

The read is offline: it opens this machine's project config and nothing else.

Usage: `fugaro project routing show [--json]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for show |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro project routing unset`

Remove the routing switch, when it carries nothing

Remove the Claude routing switch from this project's own config.

A switch that is already inert is what goes: via: direct routes nothing, so
removing it says what the file already said, and every call goes to Anthropic.
The removal is refused while the switch carries the cascade or a route, and
that refusal is the publisher's own rule about a silent node, made here: a
block that disappears from the file would turn the cascade, or a route, off by
omission on the next publish — the cascade is what hands a run the project's
other credentials, and a route that goes away is a Claude call that stops being
sent where it was put. Write the switch off on purpose instead
(`fugaro project routing set claude --via direct`), which keeps the block and
says what it means.

The change reaches a run through `fugaro update`. Only the key it removes is
rewritten: every comment and every other key of the file is kept.

Usage: `fugaro project routing unset`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for unset |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the write without a prompt |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

Show the effective project: caps, policy, allow-list, repositories running now

Print the effective project: the caps the installation's nodes carry (global,
defaults and per repository), the published policy, the allow-list with where
each entry came from, and the repositories the run registry holds. The registry
holds the runs in flight, so that list is what is running now — an empty one is

## `fugaro project sync`

Offer the provider's repositories that the allow-list does not admit

Ask the provider which repositories it holds and offer the ones the published
allow_repos does not admit, as one list written in one batch: nothing is
asked, and what was written is printed after the write. The accepted list is
written through the same ETag-guarded write `project repos add` uses; entries
are only ever added, so a sync never un-enrolls a repository — including one
the provider does not hold at all (another provider's, or one whose access was
removed). A repository the list already admits, a pattern included, is not
offered: its runs are admitted already.

The provider is GitHub's App by default: the repositories the App is installed
on, read with the App's own credentials. Reading the App's private key is
--github-app-key: without it, nothing is read. Under it the key is read from
the project's github-app-key secret with your own credentials and held in
memory only to sign the App's 9-minute JWT (never printed, never passed as an
argument, never in an error), and the flag is refused in a coding agent's
session. The App ID is a number, not a secret: --github-app-id, or the one
this machine's config already holds.

--bitbucket <workspace> lists that workspace's repositories instead, through
Bitbucket's own API, and --bitbucket-project narrows the listing to one
project of it. The token is a workspace or project access token, read from
stdin or from a hidden prompt and never from an argument — an argument is in
the process's command line, where every process on the machine reads it, and
in the shell's history — and it is held in memory only for the listing.

--check prints the difference and writes nothing, whichever provider lists:
the published allow-list is read and left exactly as it was.

Usage: `fugaro project sync [--bitbucket <workspace>] [--bitbucket-project <key>] [--check] [--github-app-id <id>] [--github-app-key] [--yes]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--bitbucket` | string | "" | no | list this Bitbucket workspace's repositories instead of the GitHub App's, with a Bitbucket access token read from stdin or a hidden prompt (never from an argument) |
| `--bitbucket-project` | string | "" | no | narrow --bitbucket to one project of that workspace (its project key) |
| `--check` | bool | `false` | no | print what would be added and write nothing |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `--github-app-id` | string | "" | no | the GitHub App's ID (a number, not a secret); default: the one this machine's config holds |
| `--github-app-key` | bool | `false` | no | read the project's GitHub App private key from Secret Manager to ask GitHub (your own credentials; refused in a coding agent's session) |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for sync |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | accepted and does nothing: the batch is written with no confirmation |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro reaper`

Sweep the Batch jobs and VMs a run has leaked

One pass of the reaper (docs/design/compute-backend.md §3.4): delete the Batch jobs
that are stuck or queued past their deadline, and the Compute Engine instances of runs
no Batch job accounts for, in this project and region.

The reaper holds five permissions and creates nothing (SECURITY.md). Every deletion
rests on a label check of its own, and anything it cannot explain it refuses to touch --
naming it in the report, which is what this command prints and what its own Cloud Run
job logs.

Run it as the installation's reaper account. --dry-run prints the same report and
deletes nothing.

Where no project config is selected the pass reads the reaper job's own environment
(FUGARO_GCP_PROJECT and FUGARO_REGION, which Terraform sets on the job), and deletes
only inside the Cloud Run job that also sets FUGARO_REAPER_JOB: anywhere else that
environment is a dry run, so an operator's shell never sweeps their project.

Two GCP projects are refused by name wherever they are named from, and an installation
may add its own to the list with FUGARO_REAPER_REFUSE_PROJECTS (comma-separated project
ids): the pass refuses those before it opens a client, so nothing is read and nothing
deleted.

Usage: `fugaro reaper`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--dry-run` | bool | `false` | no | print what would be deleted, and delete nothing |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for reaper |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

## `fugaro report`

Report what the project spent, by day, week, month, year, repository, model, person or mode

Report model spend from the project's spend history.

Finished days are read from the spendDaily documents in the project's Firebase
Firestore (you need roles/datastore.viewer on the Firebase project, which
launchers, operators and budget admins have). Today, yesterday and any day the
daily job has not archived yet are computed live from the budget database and
marked (partial). --since and --until are UTC dates (YYYY-MM-DD); --since also
takes Nd, the last N days up to --until (default 30d); --until defaults to today.

--by day|week|month|year groups in time; weeks are ISO weeks in UTC, starting on
Monday (2026-W40). --by repo|model|person groups across the range, and --by mode
groups by the rigor mode each run resolved (poc, startup, pro, critical, hotfix,
and none for a run whose record carries no mode, or carries one this version does
not know), read from the run records and not from this history: a mode row made
only of runs whose records could not be read is marked unreadable and reads n/a,
never 0. Dollars are exact (integer micro-dollars). Model $, NOTIONAL~ (a
subscription's list-price figure, never billed) and COMPUTE $ are separate
columns and never summed; compute reads n/a when no run's compute was estimated.
A person is the stored requester address; `unknown` is spend, and runs, with no
requester recorded. By model, a subscription model's dollars are notional
(priced from its tokens, so they can differ slightly from the run's recorded
notional total).

--csv writes RFC 4180 with spreadsheet-safe cells (a cell starting with = + - @
is prefixed with '). --json prints {project, source, degraded, by, since, until,
weeks, rows[{key, start, end, partial, unreadable, model_micros, model_usd,
notional_micros, notional_usd, compute_micros, compute_usd, compute_estimated,
run_hours, runs, calls, tokens}], totals, warnings}; *_usd are exact decimal
strings and null means n/a or not recorded for that breakdown (an unreadable
row carries null money).

A project without Firestore history says so and shows run-record totals instead
(from the runs bucket, not budget history).

Usage: `fugaro report`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--by` | string | `day` | no | group by day, week, month, year, repo, model, person or mode |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--csv` | bool | `false` | no | print CSV (RFC 4180) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for report |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | only this repository (owner/name) |
| `--since` | string | `30d` | no | first day: YYYY-MM-DD (UTC) or Nd, the last N days |
| `--until` | string | "" | no | last day, YYYY-MM-DD (UTC; default today) |
