## `fugaro restore`

Rebuild a managed project from zero, into a new GCP project ID, and print what is not restored

Rebuild a managed project from zero into a NEW GCP project ID.

A managed project is one fugaro created, with a marker and an owner-written
delete list. When it is lost — deleted, or closed — its ID stays reserved for
about thirty days, so this is a restore into a new project:

  - NEW_PROJECT_ID is the GCP project the installation is rebuilt in. It is
    created through the same path fugaro setup --create-project --managed uses,
    which is also what re-marks the project as managed and re-creates the
    deployer account with the rest of the installation, so neither is a
    separate step here. The repository's gcp_project: line is moved to it, so
    teammates find the shared config again.
  - ROOT is the repository's agent-authored Terraform root, in the checkout
    whose fugaro.yaml names the project. It is applied from zero through the
    SAME path fugaro managed apply runs — the managed allowlist, the
    deterministic gate over the saved plan, the owner's delete list, and the
    deployer account of D75 — into the dedicated state bucket the new project
    was created with. No prior state is read: the state lived in the project
    that was lost.

The OLD project's own creation fact is read whenever the old project can
still be read: a project that is not managed is refused, whatever flags are
given, and a managed one gives the monthly budget amount unless --budget and
--budget-currency are given. When the old project cannot be read (deleted,
closed, not yours to read) the restore proceeds only on --budget and
--budget-currency. The billing account is always yours to give: the creation
fact is not a credential and records none.

NEW_PROJECT_ID must not exist: an existing project is refused (Fugaro only starts fresh).
If the creation fails or does not end in a project this run created and
marked, the local project config file is put back as it was and the restore
can be run again; what the creation did in the cloud (the project, its
billing link, its state bucket, the installation's resources, any secrets)
is not undone, and the message says so.

Every step is money or permanent, so this command prints what it is about to
make permanent — the new project, the budget amount, the root and the two files
— before its first write, and the creating path it delegates to keeps its own
typed questions (the new project's ID and the billing account) at a real
terminal. There is no --yes, no --non-interactive and no address argument. The
command is refused in a coding agent's session.

It ends by printing what was NOT restored, as a list: the runs that were in
flight and their counters, the spend history and the kill-switch state, the
Firestore and RTDB application data, the Firestore database's location (which
is permanent and can never be changed), every secret value, the plan files
that were never stored, and the owner-written delete list — fugaro/allow-delete.json
is not carried across and nothing here re-creates it, so until the owner writes
it again with fugaro allow-delete every delete and replace in the new project
is refused (D74). The project layer and the project's recipes are not held by
the repository and are not re-published: the command names them and the one
command that publishes each. The deployer account is the one thing that is
re-created rather than lost, and the output says so.

Usage: `fugaro restore NEW_PROJECT_ID ROOT`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--billing-account` | string | "" | no | the billing account the new project is linked to (required: the creation fact records the amount and no account) |
| `--budget` | int64 | `0` | no | the new project's monthly budget amount, in whole units of --budget-currency (default: the amount the OLD project's creation fact records) |
| `--budget-currency` | string | "" | no | the budget's currency, such as USD (travels with --budget) |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--display-name` | string | "" | no | with the creation: the new project's display name (default: its ID) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for restore |
| `--parent` | string | "" | no | with the creation: organizations/<number> or folders/<number> to create the project under (default: no parent; an organization is never guessed) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro review`

Review a pull request in a job of its own, on a named account

Launch an independent review of pull request N, in a container the coding
run never ran in and with the account you name.

The review runs on the review-only variant of the repository's job: no App
key, no Claude token and no signing key are mounted in it, and its git
credential is a read-only one it fetches from the installation's credentials
service. It reads a fresh clone of the pull request's head, writes its verdict
as an artifact (fugaro review show RUN prints it) and posts no comment and no
review on the pull request: what reaches the pull request is the owner's and
the coordinator's to decide.

The account is picked as everywhere else: --token, else agent.oauth_token in
fugaro.yaml at the run's ref, else the project's default_claude_account.

--mutate FILE:TEST asks for one mutation check: the reviewer flips a boolean
literal in FILE, which must be Go source in the head under review, and TEST —
a Go test name — must then fail. The artifact carries what was observed; it is
evidence and never a verdict.

--json prints the launch's own result, the run id, its job and the account, as
every other command's --json does. The verdict does not exist yet: it is
written by the job, and `fugaro review show RUN` reads it back.

A pull request whose own coding run is still going is refused: the review
records the head it read, and a head that moves under it would leave the
verdict about a commit that is no longer there.

Usage: `fugaro review --pr N`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for review |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--mutate` | stringArray | `[]` | no | ask for one mutation check, as <file:test>: the Go source in the reviewed head to flip and the Go test name that must then fail; at most one |
| `--pr` | int | `0` | no | the pull request to review (required) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--token` | string | "" | no | named Claude account (claude_accounts in the local config) this review runs as; default: agent.oauth_token in fugaro.yaml at the run's ref, else the project's default_claude_account |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro review show` -- Print a review run's verdict artifact and its markdown

## `fugaro review show`

Print a review run's verdict artifact and its markdown

Print what a review run wrote: its verdict artifact (review.json), and the
same review rendered as markdown (review.md). RUN is <repo-slug>/<run-id>.

--json prints the artifact's own JSON alone, byte for byte as the review job
wrote it, so the bytes are the ones the service signed and a reader that
checks the signature (the sidecar object review.json.sig) is checking those
bytes.

A run that is still going has no artifact yet; the command says so rather than
printing an empty review.

Usage: `fugaro review show RUN`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for show |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print the artifact's own JSON alone, exactly as the review job wrote it |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

## `fugaro rigor`

Set the rigor mode a project's runs are held to

The rigor mode decides how much review a run gets and what it costs.

`fugaro rigor set <mode>` writes `defaults.rigor.default` of this machine's own
project layer file, and `--area <glob>` writes one rule of
`defaults.rigor.areas` — the mode a run touching that glob is held to, which is
the strictest of the rules that match it. The file is the one `fugaro update`
publishes, and every write ends with `next: fugaro update`.

A mode is `poc`, `startup`, `pro`, `critical` or `hotfix`, and `hotfix` is the one
no layer sets: it is an operator's per-run mode, reached with
`fugaro run --mode hotfix`. A mode below what the project resolves to today is
the sensitive direction, so a coding agent's session is refused it with the
command to run at your own terminal, and your own terminal writes it and asks
nothing.

Usage: `fugaro rigor`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for rigor |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro rigor floor` -- Set or remove the review floor a project's runs are held to
- `fugaro rigor set` -- Write the project layer's rigor default, or one area rule

## `fugaro rigor floor`

Set or remove the review floor a project's runs are held to

The review floor is the owner's own: per rigor mode, the review levels a run
of that mode must run whatever a lower layer asks for. It lives in this
machine's project config (`review_floor`) and `fugaro project policy publish`
copies it into the policy node the runner fails closed on, so a change here
reaches runs at the next `fugaro update`.

`fugaro rigor floor show` prints the floor this machine's config sets,
`fugaro rigor floor set MODE LEVELS` writes one mode's floor and
`fugaro rigor floor unset MODE` removes it. A removal and a lowering are the
owner's own step — a floor is a minimum, so taking a level away is a whole
project reviewing less — and they ask nothing: the write prints what it widens
and what it writes, and no flag stands in for the owner's own hand. Adding a
mode the file does not carry, or a level a mode's floor does not carry, asks
nothing either: it can only require more review.

A coding agent's session is refused both directions outright, whatever the
flags say, and is shown neither the diff nor the sentence: the command it
should run at the owner's own terminal is what the refusal prints.

Usage: `fugaro rigor floor`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for floor |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro rigor floor set` -- Write one rigor mode's review floor
- `fugaro rigor floor show` -- Show the review floor this machine's project config sets
- `fugaro rigor floor unset` -- Remove one rigor mode's review floor

## `fugaro rigor floor set`

Write one rigor mode's review floor

Write the review levels a run of MODE must run, into this machine's project
config.

LEVELS is a comma-separated list of `l1`, `l2` and `l3` — the levels
docs/review-levels names — and the floor is the whole list: a level it drops
stops being required of every run of that mode.

Adding a mode the file does not carry, or a level the mode's floor does not
carry, is the ordinary write and asks nothing. Dropping a level is a lowering —
a whole project reviewing less — and it asks nothing either: `--yes` does
not stand in for the owner's own hand, and neither does anything else. The
command refuses an empty LEVELS: a floor with no level in it says nothing, and
removing the mode's entry is what `fugaro rigor floor unset` is for.

A coding agent's session is refused the write outright, whatever the flags say,
and is shown neither the diff nor the sentence.

It writes one file: this machine's own project config. The change reaches the
policy node the runner reads at the next `fugaro update`, whose policy stage
publishes it.

Usage: `fugaro rigor floor set MODE LEVELS`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for set |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | accepted and of no effect: a lowering asks nothing, and no flag stands in for the owner's own hand |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro rigor floor show`

Show the review floor this machine's project config sets

Show the review floor, one line per rigor mode and the levels that mode's runs
must run.

The read tells apart the two ways a file can name no floor, because they mean
different things at publish: a file that says nothing about `review_floor` leaves
the published floor standing — a publish keeps the node's floor when the config
is silent about one — while a written `review_floor: {}` is a floor of nothing,
which is what takes the published floor away.

`--json` prints the same answer as a document.

Usage: `fugaro rigor floor show`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for show |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro rigor floor unset`

Remove one rigor mode's review floor

Remove the review floor MODE carries: from the next `fugaro update` the
mode's runs are held to what their rigor mode and the repository ask for, and
to nothing the owner requires.

That is what the removal of one of several modes does. Removing the file's LAST
entry leaves the file carrying no mode, and the key stays where it was written
as the empty mapping — `review_floor: {}` — rather than going with it, because
the two spellings mean different things at publish: a file that says nothing
about the key keeps the node's floor (the floor is the member a publish must not
lower by accident), while the empty mapping is a floor of nothing, and that is
what takes the published floor away.

A removal is the owner's own step — what it deletes is a floor, and taking it
away is a whole project reviewing less — and it asks nothing: `--yes` does
not stand in for the owner's own hand, and neither does anything else. A
coding agent's session is refused the removal outright, whatever the flags say,
and is shown neither the diff nor the sentence.

It writes one file: this machine's own project config, and the change reaches
the policy node at the next `fugaro update`.

Usage: `fugaro rigor floor unset MODE`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for unset |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | accepted and of no effect: a removal asks nothing, and no flag stands in for the owner's own hand |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro rigor set`

Write the project layer's rigor default, or one area rule

Write a rigor mode into this machine's own project layer file.

With no --area the command writes `defaults.rigor.default`: the mode every run of
this project starts from unless an area rule or a repository's own file moves
it. With --area GLOB it writes one rule of `defaults.rigor.areas`: a glob a rule
already carries has its mode replaced, and a glob the layer does not carry yet
is added and then needs --name — the rule's name is what the run record and the
pull request say decided the mode. --name on a rule the layer already carries
renames it. A second rule with the same glob is refused: one glob addresses one
rule, and two rules matching one path leave only the strictest of them deciding.

A mode below what this project resolves to today is the sensitive direction: a
coding agent's session is refused it with the diff and the command to run at
your own terminal, `--yes` included, and your own terminal writes it and asks
nothing. `hotfix` is refused in either form, naming `fugaro run --mode hotfix`.

The command prints the review floor beside the write, and it cannot lower it:
the floor is outside every layer, and `fugaro rigor floor` is the command that
changes one.

It writes one file: this machine's own project layer file, whose path is
derived from the selected project's name. A project that has published no layer
and has no local file of its own gets one — a project layer document carrying
this installation's anchors and the change that was asked for — so a fresh
installation can set a mode. A project that HAS published a layer is not written
over: with no local file there the command refuses and names `fugaro update`,
whose Layer stage seeds the file from that layer.

Usage: `fugaro rigor set MODE [--area GLOB [--name NAME]]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--area` | string | "" | no | write this glob's rule in defaults.rigor.areas instead of the layer's default (e.g. docs/**) |
| `--ask` | bool | `false` | no | in a project whose marks say it is managed, ask the confirmation this write would otherwise get instead of writing on the gate's verdict: a managed project asks nothing by default, and this is the flag that puts the question back. Refused where nobody can answer it (a coding agent's session, a pipe, --non-interactive); a no-op with a sentence in a project that is not managed; refused beside --yes |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for set |
| `--name` | string | "" | no | the rule's name; required for a glob the layer does not carry yet, and a rename for one it does |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the write without a prompt |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro run`

Launch a task in the cloud; it always ends with a PR

Launch a task in the cloud. The task is TEXT or --task-file (- for stdin).

A repeated --run-id reports the existing launch instead of starting another, so
a caller that is unsure whether its launch went through can simply repeat it.
--retry RUN launches a run whose task was stored but never started.

--pr N continues Fugaro's pull request N: the run acts on the PR's review comments
by the authors fugaro.yaml's followup.trusted lists, on the PR's own branch, with
the base branch and workflow of the runs before it. TEXT, or --task-file, is
optional then, and adds instructions.

--recipe NAME --pr N, NAME naming a mode: review recipe such as review-only or pick,
reviews any open pull request of the repository instead (not only Fugaro's own) and
never pushes or opens one; repeat --pr (2 to 4 times) for pick, which compares them.
TEXT, or --task-file, is optional then too, and adds instructions to the review.

--attempts N (2 to 4) launches N independent runs of the same task as a best-of-N
batch, under one batch label (bestof-<first run id> unless --batch is given); once
they have all opened a pull request, compare them with fugaro run --recipe pick.
It takes no --pr, --run-id or --retry.

--title TEXT names the run: one line, at most 100 characters. It is what
fugaro watch and runs ls list the run by, and the title (with the body's first
heading) of the pull request the run opens when the agent writes no pr.md of
its own. Without it the run is named by the task's first line, so briefs that
start with the same preamble all read alike. A follow-up (--pr) keeps its run's
title unless --title is given, and --retry takes none (the stored task keeps its
own).

--plan-task PLAN/TASK records which task of which plan this run works on, so
the console's graph can join the run to that node. One plan and one task id,
as the plan's own graph spells them, at most 128 bytes; what the run does is
unchanged by it. A follow-up (--pr) records one only when it is given, and
--retry takes none (the stored task keeps its own).

--no-compression turns the repository's agent.compression off for this run only,
overriding its fugaro.yaml. There is no --compression flag: turning compression
on is a reviewed fugaro.yaml change. A follow-up (--pr) keeps its run's choice,
and --retry takes none (the stored task keeps its own).

--mode MODE asks for a rigor mode for this run: poc, startup, pro, critical, hotfix.
It may raise the mode the run resolves from its own configuration
(rigor.default and rigor.areas in fugaro.yaml, the project layer's defaults)
and never lower it, so a launch that asks for less cannot outvote a repository
that asked for more. A follow-up (--pr) keeps the mode the PR's runs recorded
and may only raise it: asking for less is refused, and so is hotfix, which
only an operator's own run reaches. --path PATH declares a path this run will
touch, repeatable, matched against those area rules before the run starts;
without either flag a first run resolves from its configuration alone, and a
follow-up from that and the mode it keeps. Both are
recorded in the run's record and named in the pull request's status line.

Usage: `fugaro run [TEXT]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--attach` | stringArray | `[]` | no | attach a file to the run: repeatable, uploaded to the run's own inputs/ and downloaded by a mode: artifact run into the checkout's inputs/ (needs a mode: artifact recipe; refused on a run ID that already has a task) |
| `--attempts` | int | `0` | no | launch N (2 to 4) independent runs of the same task, workflow, ref and recipe as a best-of-N batch (bestof-<first run id> unless --batch is given); refused with --pr, --run-id, --retry or a review-mode recipe |
| `--batch` | string | "" | no | batch label, to group runs in fugaro runs ls |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--continues` | string | "" | no | continue the chain of RUN (a run ID, or <repo-slug>/<run-id>): this launch inherits the chain's remaining limits, for a chain with no pull request — the run you name opened nothing to follow up. The chain's limit is read from the run that began it, and what it has spent from the chain's runs' budget ledgers; this launch's own --max-* may only tighten the remaining. Refused with --pr, --retry and --attempts, which name a chain's previous run themselves |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for run |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--max-review-rounds` | string | "" | no | cap this chain's review rounds at N, senior-review iterations included: tighten-only, and never refused against the mode's own number — the rounds a run spends stay the mode's and the recipe's, and this bounds the whole chain |
| `--max-time` | string | "" | no | cap this chain's elapsed run time, as a duration such as 45m or 2h: --total-timeout keeps its own meaning and may raise this run's clock, and the two compose as the smaller of the two (the run's clock is min(--total-timeout, this)) |
| `--max-tokens` | string | "" | no | cap this chain's token total at N tokens, such as 900000: tighten-only, like --max-usd, and recorded in the task's overrides |
| `--max-usd` | string | "" | no | cap this chain's model spend at X dollars, such as 5 or 12.5: it may only tighten the ceiling this launch resolves (fugaro refuses a looser value and names the layer that set the lower one), and it is recorded in the task's overrides, beside the total_timeout that is there today. A chain is the run that sets it and the runs that continue it; a launch that names no such limit gets today's per-run caps and no chain at all |
| `--mode` | string | "" | no | the rigor mode to ask for: poc, startup, pro, critical, hotfix; it may raise the mode the run resolves from its configuration (rigor.default, rigor.areas, the project layer) and never lower it; a follow-up (--pr) keeps the mode the PR's runs recorded and may only raise it, and takes no hotfix; without it a first run resolves from those layers alone, and a follow-up from those and the mode it keeps |
| `--no-budget-check` | bool | `false` | no | skip the launch pre-check of the budget (kill switches, missing caps, no headroom); the run is held to the same limits when it starts |
| `--no-compression` | bool | `false` | no | turn agent.compression off for this run only, overriding fugaro.yaml; there is no flag to turn it on, which is a reviewed fugaro.yaml change |
| `--owner-ruled` | string | "" | no | the repository owner's ruling on the findings a run on this PR left for them (OD1): either the text itself, a file, or - for stdin. A follow-up on a pull request whose last run stopped waiting on owner decisions is refused without it, and one whose last run left no such decisions is refused with it: the ruling answers what that run left, and nothing else; it is appended to this run's brief verbatim and recorded in the run |
| `--path` | stringArray | `[]` | no | declare a path this run will touch, matched against the rigor.areas rules in effect (the repository's, and the project layer's beside them): repeatable; a run that declares none matches no area rule |
| `--plan-task` | string | "" | no | record the plan task this run works on, as <plan>/<task> (for example setup-wizard/W1.3): the id the console's graph joins this run to a node by; it changes nothing about what the run does, and a follow-up (--pr) records one only when given |
| `--pr` | intSlice | `[]` | no | continue Fugaro PR N: act on its trusted review comments (TEXT adds instructions); with a mode: review --recipe, review PR N instead (repeatable, 1 to 4, any open PR) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--recipe` | string | "" | no | the recipe (task loop) to run: .fugaro/recipes/NAME.yaml, the project's, or the catalog's (ab-judge, default, escalate, lint-fix, pick, premium, rebase, review-only, run-digest, solo, standard, test-and-fix); default: agent.recipe in fugaro.yaml, else default; a follow-up (--pr) keeps its previous run's |
| `--ref` | string | "" | no | base branch or ref the run is cut from (default: the branch this checkout is on, when origin has it and it is not the base branch; else the base branch (fugaro.yaml git.base_branch, then the local config's, then the project's base_branch, then main)) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | repository as owner/name, or a path inside its checkout (default: this checkout's origin) |
| `--retry` | string | "" | no | launch the stored task of RUN (a full run ID, or <repo-slug>/<run-id>) that never started: a run an ending names is never launched, since the bucket cannot vouch for which run an ending means |
| `--review-levels` | string | "" | no | read the run's own review levels from this YAML file, or - for stdin: the block the task stores as review_levels (l1, l2, l3, each of model, effort, none and focus), decoded strictly, with no key on no level meaning the configuration decides it. Asking for levels needs a job image whose runner acts on them, so a launch on an older one is refused and names fugaro image refresh; without the flag the run resolves its levels from its configuration and its mode alone |
| `--run-id` | string | "" | no | run ID to use; repeating one reports its launch instead of starting another |
| `--security` | bool | `false` | no | ask for the strongest review this run can get: it turns review level 3 on for the run whatever paths it changed, over the repository's own security: rows and the project layer's always_level_3. It only ever turns the level on — there is no way to ask for less — as --mode raises a mode and never lowers one, and a run that says nothing resolves its levels from its configuration alone |
| `--task-file` | string | "" | no | read the task from this file, or - for stdin |
| `--tier` | string | "" | no | the expectation tier to dispatch this run at: trivial, small, medium, large. It is what the run is expected to cost and take (governance.tiers in fugaro.yaml and the project layer), and never a cap: the run's own budget cap stays the ceiling. A --pr follow-up keeps the tier its PR's runs recorded; without this flag a run carries no expectation at all |
| `--title` | string | "" | no | the run's title, one line: what fugaro watch and runs ls list the run by, and the pull request's title unless the agent wrote its own pr.md (default: the task's first line); a follow-up (--pr) keeps its run's title unless this is given |
| `--token` | string | "" | no | named Claude account (claude_accounts in the local config) this run uses, for a workflow whose agent.auth is oauth; default: agent.oauth_token in fugaro.yaml, else the repository's default account; a follow-up (--pr) keeps its previous run's account unless this is given explicitly, which overrides it (checked the same way as a first run's) |
| `--total-timeout` | string | "" | no | override the workflow's timeouts.total for this run, such as 45m |
| `--used-review-rounds` | string | "" | no | state that the chain has already spent N review rounds, such as 2: tighten-only like --used-usd |
| `--used-time` | string | "" | no | state that the chain has already used this much wall time, as a duration such as 45m: tighten-only like --used-usd |
| `--used-tokens` | string | "" | no | state that the chain has already used N tokens, such as 400000: tighten-only like --used-usd, and the one figure a chain whose budget is off reads for the token dimension, which no run record carries |
| `--used-usd` | string | "" | no | state that the chain has already used X dollars, such as 3 or 2.5: it may only raise what the engine read from the chain's runs (fugaro refuses a figure below it, naming both), which is how a caller accounts for spend the chain's own runs do not hold |
| `--workflow` | string | "" | no | workflow to run (default: the repo's only workflow) |

| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for runs |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro runs digest` -- Write a closed period's report of this repository into its own docs tree
- `fugaro runs ls` -- List runs with their status, stage, cost and PR
- `fugaro runs show` -- Show a run's chain and what is left of its limits

## `fugaro runs digest`

Write a closed period's report of this repository into its own docs tree

Write one closed period's report of this repository, from its run records, into
the repository's own docs tree: <dir>/<YYYY>/<key>.md, plus the index
<dir>/README.md regenerated from the files there (D321).

The report is internal/digest's: the period's runs, the flagged ones and the
dearest of the rest, the stage figures, the summary block a later report reads,
and the fixed pattern rules (D326) read over that block and the committed ones.
A yearly report has no runs of its own to read -- the records are kept 90 days
(F24) -- so it is that year's monthly reports added up, and the report says how
many of the twelve it added up, so a partial year is not read as a whole one.

--date names any day inside the period. Without it the most recent closed period
is reported: the day, week, month or year before the one today falls in. A period
holding today is still receiving runs -- a run counts in the period it finished,
in UTC (G4) -- so it is refused and nothing is written for it, and so is a period
that has not begun yet.

The report is of this repository and of no other (G2, D322): --repo names it, and
without --repo it is the checkout's own origin. There is no --all. A record under
the repository's prefix whose own repository is another is not read into the
report, and no report names another repository.

Nothing in a report is a person or a task's own words (G1, D323): the flags,
recipes and figures are internal/digest's own closed vocabulary, and a report is
committed into a repository that may be public. Nothing here refuses in a coding
agent's session, which is what makes the scheduled report run possible.

The committed reports under --dir are the ones the pattern rules read, and each is
re-checked by shape before it is used: a report a person edited by hand, or a
markdown file whose name is not <YYYY>/<key>.md, is named on stderr by its own path
and left out of the patterns and of the index's figures, and the report being
written goes on. Nothing else in the folder is read, and the folder is never edited
except for the report and the index.

The read is the repository's runs bucket listing, newest first, capped at the bound
runs stats uses, and a listing longer than that says so on stderr. The listing is not
narrowed to the period: a run counts in the period it finished (G4), so a run that
started before the period and finished inside it is one of its runs. The bucket's
lifecycle age keeps the listing small, and F24's retention means a period older than
it has no records left -- which is why a yearly report rolls the committed monthly
ones up rather than reading records.

--stdout prints the report instead of writing it, and --json prints the summary
block and the patterns as {repo, period, summary, patterns[], skipped[]}. Neither
writes a file, so a caller can read a report before committing it.

--due is the cadence's own reading: it names the periods that have closed with no
report under --dir, newest first -- the period that ended most recently is the
first line, and of two that ended on the same day the longer one comes first --
and how old the newest report it found is. It reads that folder and nothing else --
no project, no credential, no bucket -- so it answers in a checkout that has never
been set up, and it writes nothing: --period, --date, --repo, --stdout and
--submit-draft have nothing to act on beside it and are refused by name. --json
prints it as {version, dir, due[], newest}.

--submit-draft prints neither: it prints a redacted learning draft a person can
file as a "Skill learning" issue, and it sends nothing. The draft leaves the
repository, so it carries no repository name and no run ID -- a period other
than a year renumbers its runs run-1, run-2, ... (a yearly draft rolls the
months up and has no run rows) -- and it ends with the one command that opens
the issue form, gh issue create --web -R dimipaun/fugaro, which the
person runs themselves: the form lives in Fugaro's repository and -R is what
reaches it from the checkout this command read, and the person picks the
"Skill learning" form in the browser, because --web ignores --template. --dir
still names the folder the committed reports the pattern rules read live in;
nothing is written there, so --stdout and --json are refused beside it.

Usage: `fugaro runs digest`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--date` | string | "" | no | any day inside the period (YYYY-MM-DD); default: the most recent closed period |
| `--dir` | string | `docs/fugaro-reviews` | no | the folder the reports live in, relative to the working directory |
| `--due` | bool | `false` | no | print the closed periods this checkout has no report for; reads the folder and nothing else |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for digest |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print the summary block and the patterns as JSON |
| `--period` | string | `day` | no | the period to report: day, week, month or year |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | the repository to report (owner/name, or a path inside its checkout); default: this checkout's origin |
| `--stdout` | bool | `false` | no | print the report instead of writing it |
| `--submit-draft` | bool | `false` | no | print a redacted learning draft for a "Skill learning" issue; sends nothing |

## `fugaro runs ls`

List runs with their status, stage, cost and PR

List runs, newest first -- created descending, then run descending --
joining the runs bucket with what the backend knows.

By default ls shows the last 7 days of the local config's repositories (every
repository in the bucket when the config lists none). A run shows as succeeded
only when its result.json says so; an execution that ended without finalizing
is an infra_error.

--limit N prints the newest N rows of the listing and shortens nothing else:
the window is still read, and the totals line, in the text listing and in
--json's totals, is the whole window's, because a page is not a total. 0,
the default, prints every row of the window.

--after RUN-ID starts the listing after that run: the rows strictly after it
in the listing's order, so the same argv with the last id of a page is the
next page. The id is the run_id --json carries; one the listing does not
hold is refused rather than answered with an empty page, which reads as no
more runs. Neither flag goes with --watch, which redraws the whole listing.

--state STATE lists only runs in that state, matched against the status --json
carries: the `halted (run_cap)` cell is --state halted, and --help lists the
states the flag takes. A run's state is in its result.json, so this filter
reads every run it filters -- it narrows the listing, never the reads.

--debt lists only the runs filed from a triage deferral: a task whose own spec
is marked debt, which is work a run's review left behind rather than work
somebody asked for. Like --state it reads the runs it filters, since the
mark is in the run's task.json; a run whose task.json is unreadable is
left out rather than guessed in, because nothing there says it is one.

--group-by failure_class adds a block to the listing: one row per class of the
closed vocabulary, with the runs of the window that ended in it, their share
of the window's runs, and what they cost. It groups the rows the listing has
already read and reads nothing new, and it moves nothing: the rows and the
totals are the ones without it, and --json gains the `groups` block beside
them. A page of a grouped listing is a page's total, so --group-by doesn't go
with --limit, --after or --watch.

--pr N lists the runs on pull request N of one repository (the first run and
its follow-ups), over the last 90d unless --since says otherwise; the totals
line is then the PR's total cost.

Usage: `fugaro runs ls`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--after` | string | "" | no | print only the rows after this run id in the listing |
| `--all` | bool | `false` | no | every repository in the runs bucket |
| `--batch` | string | "" | no | only runs of this batch |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--debt` | bool | `false` | no | only runs filed from a triage deferral (a task marked debt) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `--group-by` | string | "" | no | group the listing by one field (failure_class) |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for ls |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--limit` | int | `0` | no | print only the newest N rows (0, the default, is every row of the window; the totals stay the window's) |
| `--mine` | bool | `false` | no | only runs you requested |
| `--pr` | int | `0` | no | only runs on this pull request (needs one repository; --since defaults to 90d) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | only this repository (owner/name, or a path inside its checkout) |
| `--since` | string | `7d` | no | only runs started within this long (7d, 36h, 90m; 0 for all) |
| `--state` | string | "" | no | only runs in this state (cancelled, error, failed, halted, infra_error, launching, pending, running, succeeded, unlaunched, unreviewed) |
| `--watch` | bool | `false` | no | redraw until every run has settled |

## `fugaro runs show`

Show a run's chain and what is left of its limits

Show the chain RUN (a run ID, <repo-slug>/<run-id>, or the last four or
more characters of a run ID) belongs to: the run that began it, each
dimension's limit, what the chain has used of it and what is left, the layer
each limit's source names, and whether the chain is ENFORCED or UNENFORCED.
When the run is halted, the halt is printed too.

A chain is the unit of work whose runs share one limit (D1045): the limit is the
figure the run that began the chain was launched with, and what has been used is
read off the chain's runs — the dollars and tokens from the budget database's
per-run ledgers, the wall time and review rounds from the run records. With the
budget off there is no ledger, the records are the figures, the chain is marked
UNENFORCED, and the token dimension is reported unmeasured rather than
approximated.

The wall-time and review-round limits are advisory: no rule enforces them.

The bucket ages a run's objects out, so a chain older than that window has a
root whose stored task is gone: the chain itself is still shown and its limit is
reported as one that could not be read (limits_read false) rather than as a chain
that bounds nothing (limits_read true, an empty limits).

--json prints {version, repo, run, chain, run_count, enforced, limits_read, limits[], halt},
each limit a {dimension, limit, used, remaining, source} whose amounts are in
the dimension's own unit: micro-dollars for the money — the unit the budget
database and the rest of the CLI's documents count it in — whole tokens,
seconds and a count.

Usage: `fugaro runs show RUN`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for show |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | the repository RUN belongs to (owner/name, or a path inside its checkout; needed only for a bare run ID) |

## `fugaro runs stats`

Aggregate run records by the person who started each run

Count the runs one installation's records hold, and what they cost, grouped by
the person who started each one: how many jobs an identity began, how they ended,
what they spent, and a total row.

The numbers come from the run records, not from the budget database: each run's
launch.json carries the launcher it recorded at launch, and its result.json the
outcome and the settled cost. Nothing else is read, no counter is consulted, and
nothing is written.

Attribution, as the records themselves state it:

  - A follow-up (fugaro run --pr) belongs to the launcher of that follow-up: the
    identity is the one the follow-up's own launch recorded.
  - An automated launch -- a service account, a CI runner -- appears as its own
    identity, exactly as it recorded itself; it is never folded into a person's.
  - A run whose launch recorded no launcher is grouped as 'unknown'. It is never
    guessed from the run's task, its record or the account it ran under.
  - Dollars are never added across currencies: a row is one user and one currency,
    and a total covers one currency. Every cost recorded today is in USD.
  - The window is UTC days like the rest of the CLI. A run is counted on the day
    the bucket's run IDs place its start, so the window and the runs in it agree
    with runs ls.

The money is model dollars, counted the way the budget screens count them. COUNTED
$ is the model spend that counts toward the caps: the money part of a run's model
figure (model_usd minus model_notional_usd, C1.16/P12). NOTIONAL $ is the part of
that figure a subscription paid -- a run on agent.auth oauth whole, and a cascade
run's tier-A calls, whose run is otherwise an api-key one -- which counts toward
the plan's limits and is no one's bill. The spend basis decides only a record
written before that breakdown existed, which is what says a figure was never
billed. They are separate columns and are never summed. Compute is not attributed
to a person: no run's compute is, and the budget database's own person view
leaves it out too. AVG
$/RUN is COUNTED $ over COUNTED RUNS, the runs that settled a real-dollar cost;
a notional run, a run with no readable record and a record from before the cost
breakdown existed are none of them averaged in as a run that cost nothing.

Who sees whom. An admin of the installation -- the identity the local config's
user: (or git config user.email) names, listed in its terraform.admins, one of
the two lists fugaro doctor's runs-bucket-iam check reads -- sees every user.
Anyone else sees their own row alone, and --all-users asks for the whole table.
An installation that names no admins (one from before the 0.7.0 hardening, say)
places nobody, and the view then stays private: the default is never the wider
one. Whose numbers a table shows is printed above it.

A private view is the caller's own row. A caller whose identity cannot be told at
all -- the local config names nobody, and git config user.email answers nothing --
is refused, never quietly widened: the error says so, and names --all-users. An
identity with no key of its own because nothing printable is left of it (a pasted
zero-width character, say) is shown no row instead: the table is empty, and its
view line says the CLI cannot tell who you are. A row keyed 'unknown' is every run
of the window that recorded no launcher -- never one person's -- so it is not shown
as the caller's own either, and a note says so.

The launcher text is what a launcher wrote and is read for nothing else: it is
sanitised and size-capped before it is printed, and it authorises and admits
nothing. Two identities that differ only in what the sanitising drops -- an
invisible character a paste left in one of them, say -- or only past the cap are
one key and one row: the row is the key, not the person. A private view is not
read off that key. It holds the runs whose launch recorded your identity itself --
the identity fugaro run writes to launch.json at launch, not the requested_by that
runs ls --mine compares -- so someone whose identity merely
sanitises to the same text is never counted in it and your own row can be
smaller than that key's row in the full table.

A window can hold every run of every repository in the bucket, so the read is
bounded: at most --max-runs records are read per call, newest first, and a window
holding more says so in the output rather than publishing figures over a part of
itself silently. The bound is on the read, not on a person: the newest --max-runs
runs are taken before any view is applied, so a private view can be over fewer of
the caller's own runs than --max-runs suggests. A run with neither a launch nor a
record -- never launched, cancelled before launch, or a stale claim -- never
started and is counted in no figure. The count of those is the window's, over
everyone's runs, and is no more the caller's own than the truncation is.

--json prints {version, project, by, view, you, admin, since, until, max_runs,
truncated, rows[], totals[], unlaunched, notes}; rows and totals carry {user,
currency, runs, succeeded, failed, halted, infra_error, other, no_record,
counted_usd, notional_usd, counted_runs, avg_counted_usd}, and the counts add up:
runs == succeeded + failed + halted + infra_error + other + no_record.

Usage: `fugaro runs stats`

Flags:

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--all` | bool | `false` | no | every repository in the runs bucket |
| `--all-users` | bool | `false` | no | show every user's row, not only your own (the table names whose numbers it shows) |
| `--by` | string | `user` | no | what to break the figures down by (user) |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for stats |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |

| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | only this repository (owner/name, or a path inside its checkout) |
| `--since` | string | `7d` | no | only runs started within this long (7d, 36h, 90m; 0 for all) |

## `fugaro runs summary`

Count the window's runs and their spend, without reading a run object

Count the runs of a window by repository and by state, and total what they
spent, from the budget database and the spend history alone.

The figures come from the day counters the caps are enforced against: the
budget database's spend, outcomes and runs nodes for the days it still holds,
and the spend history's daily documents for the days the rollover has
archived. No run object is read, so no run's task, result or transcript is
opened and the runs bucket is never listed: this is the read a listing cannot
be, and it answers in about a second over the database's own window.

A run is counted on the UTC day the database recorded its spend, which is the
day the rollover files it under, so the window and the counts agree with the
budget and not necessarily with runs ls, whose rows are the runs bucket's.
Runs that have not settled are counted in runs and in no state. SPENT is the
model money the caps count; NOTIONAL is the part a subscription paid, which
counts toward the plan's limits and is nobody's bill. The two are separate and
are never summed. COMPUTE is what the runs whose compute was priced came to,
and is n/a when no run's compute is known: this read opens no bucket, so a live
day's compute is never estimated here, and 'not estimated' is never shown as
free.

An unknown day is named, never counted as zero. The budget database holds the
days it has not pruned (today and the 8 before it); every older day is
the spend history's to answer, and a project whose history cannot answer at all
-- no Firebase backend, no database, no history mark -- names the days it
cannot know in days_unknown and counts nothing on them. A day inside the
database's window with no node is a day nothing ran on, which is known.

A window is a span of UTC days ending today: --since 7d is today and the six
days before it. The whole history is not a window, so --since 0 is refused.

--json prints {v, project, since, until, repositories[], totals, days_unknown,
notes}; repositories and totals carry {slug, repo, runs, states{}, spent_micros,
notional_micros, compute_micros, compute_runs}, and states carries all of
succeeded, failed, halted, cancelled, infra_error and other.

Usage: `fugaro runs summary`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for summary |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | only this repository (owner/name, or a path inside its checkout) |
| `--since` | string | `7d` | no | the window of UTC days ending today (7d, 36h, 90m; a summary is per day, so 0 is refused) |

## `fugaro seats`

Estimate how many people a subscription's seat rule would count

Estimate how many people a subscription's seat rule would count on this
installation, from the installation's own data alone: the people on this
machine's operator and admin lists, plus everyone who requested a run in the
last 90 days, each counted once.

The estimate is ADVISORY. A seat is a contract pricing rule of the Subscription
Terms -- anyone who launches jobs, by any means (console, mobile, CLI, an agent)
-- and nothing in the product can count one: the licence's seat is one person,
no surface knows who a person is, and every identity a run records is
self-declared. So this command reads and prints, and that is all: it stores
nothing, sends nothing, and consults no key, licence or server. It is core MIT
and reads only core data.

The three sources, and what each one is worth:

  - terraform.operators and terraform.admins in this machine's own project
    config: the two lists fugaro setup writes and fugaro update applies. They are
    the admins' record of who holds a role, and members the console or an agent
    launch records elsewhere are not in them.
  - The requesters of the runs the last 90 days minted, read from each run's
    task.json in every repository of the installation's bucket. Everyone who
    launches counts, an agent launch is recorded under the configured person, and
    an agent with no configured identity is invisible here.

What the estimate cannot tell, it lists and does not guess:

  - A group: or domain: member of either list names an unknown number of people.
    It is listed apart, with the lists that hold it, and counted nowhere: one
    seat is not a safe reading of a group, and neither is none.
  - A serviceAccount: member is one identity and no person, so it is listed and
    not counted: the licence's seat is one person, and this command never decides
    that a person holds a robot's account.
  - A run's requester is a value the launching CLI wrote down and nothing
    verifies, and an agent launch with no configured identity records none: the
    window counts whoever the records name.
  - The window is the last 90 days of run IDs, so a person whose runs are all
    older is invisible unless a list names them. The estimate over the whole
    installation is therefore a lower bound, never a ceiling.

One identity is one row. The lists and the runs spell an address
independently -- one is an IAM member a person was written to, the other is
what the launching CLI typed -- so the comparison folds case, and the row's key
is the text printed: two texts that print alike are one person, and the
estimate is the number of rows.

--json prints {version, project, days, since, until, people[], not_counted[],
unreadable, notes}; people carry {person, sources[]} and not_counted {member,
why, sources[]}, sources from run_operator, admin and requester, and why is
unknown_size or account.

Version 2 is this document. Version 1 named a row's sources with the words the
roles carried before they were renamed -- "launcher" for the run-starters and
"operator" for the admins -- and neither word is a value here any more: a
consumer reading "operator" as the list version 1 named it would draw the
admins.

## `fugaro secrets`

Store, list and withdraw a repository's secrets in Secret Manager

Usage: `fugaro secrets`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for secrets |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro secrets allow` -- Add repositories to a project secret's allow-list (project_secrets.NAME.allow_data_to)
- `fugaro secrets deny` -- Remove repositories from a project secret's allow-list
- `fugaro secrets ls` -- List the project's (or, with --repo, a repository's) secrets: names, scope and versions, never values
- `fugaro secrets rm` -- Withdraw a project secret: delete its Secret Manager container and its config entry
- `fugaro secrets set` -- Store a secret's value, read from stdin or a hidden prompt, as a new version
- `fugaro secrets shared` -- Store, list and remove the secrets the project shares (an admin's)
- `fugaro secrets user` -- Store, list and remove the secrets you own

## `fugaro secrets allow`

Add repositories to a project secret's allow-list (project_secrets.NAME.allow_data_to)

Add each PATTERN to project_secrets.NAME.allow_data_to — or to
workflow_secrets.NAME.allow_data_to for a name your local config holds there —
the list of repositories the value is stored for and mounted in.

A PATTERN is a repository as owner/name, and may use * inside a segment, never
across /: myworkspace/* is a whole workspace and myworkspace/api-* a family,
while the owner segment is literal (one project secret is one owner's
credential). A pattern means every repository it matches, now and later, so
adding one is a widening: it is one more repository the value is mounted in.

With --proxy, and no PATTERN, this writes project_secrets.NAME.proxy on its
own: the Bitbucket token's switch for the credentials service, which is also a
widening, because it hands the token to the service rather than to the job.
--proxy=false takes the switch away again and is the one form here that is not
a widening. --proxy is refused for a workflow secret, whose entry holds no such
member (D493, D1275).

Adding a repository or turning the switch on is the owner's own step: it asks
nothing at your own terminal, and a coding agent's session is refused it, with
the command to run yourself (D1552). This whole family is refused in a session,
so --yes does not lift it. Nothing here reads or prints a value.

This is a local file edit. It ends on one line: next: fugaro update — the
published policy's entry is derived from this list, so the change reaches the
project's runs in that run and not before it.

Usage: `fugaro secrets allow NAME PATTERN...`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for allow |
| `--proxy` | bool | `false` | no | set project_secrets.NAME.proxy, the Bitbucket token's switch for the credentials service (--proxy=false turns it off) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the policy write without a prompt (outside a coding agent's session) |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro secrets deny`

Remove repositories from a project secret's allow-list

Remove each PATTERN from project_secrets.NAME.allow_data_to — or from
workflow_secrets.NAME.allow_data_to for a name your local config holds there —
so the value is no longer stored for it and no longer mounted in it.

This is the one edit of this family that narrows: the repositories that remain
are the ones the value still reaches. A pattern the entry does not name is not
an error and not a write — the command says there is no change, because the
state it was asked for is the state the file is in.

A removal that leaves the list empty is allowed and is not a removal of the
entry: the value is then stored for no repository, and the entry stays for the
day a pattern is added back.

This whole family is refused in a coding agent's session, --yes included (spec
§5): what a secret reaches is a decision no plan shows. Nothing here reads or
prints a value.

This is a local file edit. It ends on one line: next: fugaro update — the
published policy's entry is derived from this list, so the change reaches the
project's runs in that run and not before it.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for deny |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the policy write without a prompt (outside a coding agent's session) |

## `fugaro secrets ls`

List the project's (or, with --repo, a repository's) secrets: names, scope and versions, never values

List secrets: their logical names, IDs, version counts and where each
value comes from, never any value (this command has no access call at all).

The default listing is the installation's project-wide containers -- the
scope secrets set stores to by default for a name that has one -- one row
per name, with the repositories the local config allows to use each one
(bitbucket-token has no project-wide default: a repository access token
serves one repository, so it is listed here only when an operator has stored
a workspace or project access token project-wide, which the
project_secrets.bitbucket-token allow-list opens).
--project-wide is accepted as a synonym, so existing scripts keep working.

--repo (or a bare --repo, for this checkout's origin) lists one repository
instead: its own containers, each with SCOPE repo (the repository's own
container), project (a project-wide container this repository may use and
has no copy of), or "project, repo override stored" (both exist; the
repository's own version wins). Nothing about a repository is listed
without --repo: the project's containers are not one repository's.

In a --repo listing, MISSING marks a name a job of that repository needs
and no enabled version resolves for: the answer to "which required secret
is gone" after a restore. "Required" is what the jobs of the repository's workflows mount and
cannot run without, worked out from the checkout's fugaro.yaml the way a
deploy works it out: the git credential of its provider, the model
credentials its agent.auth names (claude-oauth-token and each allowed
claude_accounts token for oauth; each allowed model provider's key for
api-key; none for vertex), and each workflows.<w>.secrets name.
anthropic-api-key is never marked: the job mounts it only when it has a
version and runs without it, and fugaro validate says when a pinned model
needs it. A required name with nothing behind it gets a row of its own — a
missing secret has no container to be listed from, so its SECRET, LATEST and
CREATED read "-" (in --json its id is empty and it has no created). The same
marks a container that exists with no enabled version behind it, which
resolves to nothing as surely as no container at all. Run this from a
checkout of the repository: only its fugaro.yaml says what is required, so
elsewhere, or with a fugaro.yaml that does not parse, nothing is marked and a
note on stderr says so.

The default (project-wide) listing has no MISSING column: a name absent
there may be stored per repository and perfectly present.

Usage: `fugaro secrets ls`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for ls |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--project-wide` | bool | `false` | no | the default for a name that has a project-wide meaning, accepted as a synonym so existing scripts keep working (cannot be combined with --repo) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | work on one repository's own copy, given as owner/name or a path inside its checkout (no value: this checkout's origin); without it, a name that has a project-wide meaning is stored and listed project-wide |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro secrets rm`

Withdraw a project secret: delete its Secret Manager container and its config entry

Delete the project-wide secret NAME and the local config entry that makes it
reachable.

NAME is stored once for the whole Fugaro project — in project_secrets, or in
workflow_secrets for a name your local config holds there — and this is the
command that takes it back: it deletes the Secret Manager container, with
every version in it, and removes the entry that made it reachable from your
local config in the same run, behind one confirmation and one diff.

Both halves go, and neither is left behind: an entry whose container is gone
promises a value no job can mount, and a container with no entry is a value
the project still holds after its owner asked for it to be withdrawn.

The entry removed is the one the name has: project_secrets.NAME for a
reserved name, workflow_secrets.NAME for a workflow secret. Only those two
blocks are this command's — a provider's key or a Claude account's token
shares the container's derived ID and is refused, since that name's entry is
not here to remove.

Deleting the container revokes nothing retroactively. A repository whose own
copy has an enabled version keeps using it, and a job already deployed keeps
the mount it was applied with until its next update — the command says which
repositories of this project hold their own copy.

This command never prints a value: the entry it removes holds an allow-list
and a switch, and a value is not a setting and is never in a diff.

Run it at your own terminal: a removal of a secret is a value no plan shows,
so a coding agent's session is refused, --yes included.

Usage: `fugaro secrets rm NAME`

Flags:

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| `--dry-run` | bool | `false` | no | print what the removal would do and write nothing |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for rm |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print the dry run's document as JSON (with --dry-run) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the removal without a prompt |

## `fugaro secrets set`

Store a secret's value, read from stdin or a hidden prompt, as a new version

Store the value of the repository's secret NAME as a new version in Secret
Manager, creating the secret if it doesn't exist.

NAME is one of anthropic-api-key, bitbucket-token, claude-oauth-token, github-app-key,
the secret of a model provider in the local config's providers block (for a
repository that provider's allow_data_to lists), or a secret some workflow
declares under secrets: in the repository's fugaro.yaml (run it from a
checkout of the repository for those).

The value is read only from stdin: pipe or redirect it in
(fugaro secrets set bitbucket-token < token-file), or, when stdin is a
terminal, paste it at a hidden prompt. It is never taken from an argument,
a flag or the environment, and never printed. One trailing newline (\n or
\r\n) is dropped, and the command says so. Values must be 4 bytes to
64 KiB, on one line except for github-app-key (a PEM, which must be
redirected from a file), and a one-line value may not start or end with
whitespace (a copy-and-paste slip, so it is refused rather than stored). Ctrl-C at the prompt stores nothing and restores the terminal.

Scope: with neither flag, a NAME that has a project-wide meaning is stored
once for the whole Fugaro project, in the project's own Secret Manager --
the API key, the GitHub App key, a model provider's own key (any provider,
allow_data_to or not), a reserved secret your local config's project_secrets
block allow-lists, a named Claude account's token whose account
allow-lists at least one repository, or a secret a workflow declares that
your local config's workflow_secrets block lists at least one repository
for. --project-wide is accepted as a synonym of that default, so existing
scripts keep working. Inside a shared job there is no IAM boundary between
repositories: the profile is the boundary. What the project copy reaches is
the name's own entry, and the store says which: a reserved name with no
project_secrets entry, and a model provider's key with no allow_data_to (or
an explicit ["*"]), reach every enrolled repository, while an entry that
names repositories -- project_secrets', workflow_secrets' or a named
account's -- reaches exactly those. A workflow's own secret is stored once
for the project only through such an entry: with no workflow_secrets entry
it stays in the repository's own container as before, and an entry present
with an empty allow_data_to is refused, since it would mount nowhere.

bitbucket-token has no project-wide default: a Bitbucket credential is
normally a repository access token, issued for one repository and usable for
no other, so it is stored in this repository's own container and every
repository is asked for its own value (docs/git-providers.md). An operator
who holds one workspace or project access token instead -- the credential
that reaches many repositories -- stores it once for the project by
allow-listing the repositories it serves in project_secrets.bitbucket-token,
usually the whole workspace (myworkspace/*). Storing it for the project is
refused unless that allow-list names the repositories it is meant for. That
path is not yet live-checked with a workspace or project token (Check 180).

Copy the project_secrets.bitbucket-token entry to every operator machine's
local config: the shared config never carries it, and without it
fugaro update --repo asks for a per-repository token.

An allow_data_to entry may use * inside a segment, never across /: a
workspace's whole list is written myworkspace/* (and myworkspace/api-* names
a family), while the owner segment must be literal -- a bare * is not
accepted, because one project secret is one owner's credential. A wildcard
means every repository it matches, now and later: onboarding one mounts the
project copy with nothing else to do.

With --repo (owner/name, or with no value for this checkout's origin) the
value is stored as the repository's own copy instead. That copy overrides
the project copy from then on: disabling its last enabled version is the
only way back.

The policy flags write the entry that decides who may mount the value,
instead of reading one:

  --allow-data-to OWNER/NAME   add a repository to
                               project_secrets.NAME.allow_data_to -- or to
                               workflow_secrets.NAME.allow_data_to for a
                               name your local config holds there -- the
                               list of repositories the value is stored for
  --proxy[=true|false]         set project_secrets.NAME.proxy, the Bitbucket
                               token's switch for the credentials service

NAME must be one of the reserved names above, or a name your local config
already holds in workflow_secrets (that block can hold no reserved name),
and --repo cannot be combined with either flag: the entry is the project's
own and no repository owns it. --proxy is refused for a workflow secret,
because no workflow_secrets entry holds the switch. Adding a repository to
the list, or turning proxy on, is a widening: it is the owner's own step,
asked nothing at your own terminal, and a coding agent's session is refused
it with the command to run yourself (D1552). --dry-run
says what the write would do and writes nothing, and --json prints that as
the settings-write document.

A value is not a setting: it has no row, it is never in a diff, and no dry
run of this command prints one. secrets set with neither policy flag is the
value write and reads the value from stdin; to store a value and change its
policy, run the command twice. A coding agent's session is refused the
policy flags outright, --yes included (spec §5), because a secret's policy is
a value no plan shows.

Usage: `fugaro secrets set NAME`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--allow-data-to` | stringSlice | `[]` | no | add a repository (owner/name) to NAME's allow_data_to — project_secrets.NAME.allow_data_to, or workflow_secrets.NAME.allow_data_to for a workflow secret — the list of repositories the value is stored for; comma-separated or repeated |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--dry-run` | bool | `false` | no | print what the policy write would do and write nothing |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for set |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--project-wide` | bool | `false` | no | the default for a name that has a project-wide meaning, accepted as a synonym so existing scripts keep working (cannot be combined with --repo) |
| `--proxy` | bool | `false` | no | set project_secrets.NAME.proxy, the Bitbucket token's switch for the credentials service (--proxy=false turns it off) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | work on one repository's own copy, given as owner/name or a path inside its checkout (no value: this checkout's origin); without it, a name that has a project-wide meaning is stored and listed project-wide |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm the policy write without a prompt (outside a coding agent's session) |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro secrets shared set`

Store a secret's value, read from stdin or a hidden prompt, through the intake

Store the value of NAME through the installation's secrets intake, as a new
version: the container is created if it doesn't exist, and a second call with
the same name rotates it.

The value is read only from stdin: pipe or redirect it in (fugaro secrets shared set
github-token < token-file), or, when stdin is a terminal, paste it at a hidden
prompt. It is never taken from an argument, a flag or the environment, and
never printed. One trailing newline (\n or \r\n) is dropped, and the command
says so. A value is one line of 4 bytes to 64 KiB with no whitespace at either
end. The one value that spans lines is the GitHub App key's PEM, and it has no
business here: `fugaro secrets set github-app-key` is the command that stores
one, and the intake's two prefixes refuse that name (R7). Ctrl-C at the prompt
stores nothing and restores the terminal.

The value travels to the intake and is written there by the intake's own
account: this command sends it over the installation's own endpoint, with the
person's own Google ID token as the caller, and holds no write of its own in
Secret Manager.

Scope: the project's own prefix, fugaro_p_<name>, which the intake serves
to an admin on the installation's derived admin list and to nobody else
(D1935, D1940). A caller who is not on it is refused by the intake, by name,
and nothing is written.

The installation's intake is deployed by `fugaro update`: an installation whose
release predates it, or one whose deployment does not answer the intake's
routes, is refused with that command as the whole upgrade.

Usage: `fugaro secrets user rm NAME`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for rm |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
